MUAC 113.5 mm
Z-score between -2 and -3
Swollen right foot, very skinny
items.why: The sign is oedema of both feet; check WFH/L and MUAC for the thinness.

items.text: Too weak to stand
items.why: A child can be weak for many reasons; this alone is not a sign of SAM.

items.text: Oedema of both feet
MUAC 120 mm and irritable

sections.title: If there is SAM: complications and the appetite test

read.text: Check a child with SAM for medical complications, and do the appetite test with RUTF.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text:
Signs of severe acute malnutrition

  • Under 6 months: oedema of both feet, or weight-for-length below -3 z-score
  • 6 months and older: oedema of both feet, or WFH/L below -3 z-score, or MUAC below 115 mm
If none is present, go on to classify. If any is present, look for complications.

cards.back: Any general danger sign or sign of severe illness, any severe (red) classification, or pneumonia with chest indrawing.
A breastfeeding or feeding problem, from the young infant chart.
No appetite: the child does not finish the RUTF in the appetite test.

read.text: The appetite test
A child may refuse RUTF because it is unfamiliar or the place is strange. Move the caregiver and child to a quiet, private area; you go too, because you must watch the child eat before you classify.

read.title: How to do the appetite test

steps.title: Prepare
steps.text: Use a separate quiet area. Explain the purpose of the test and how it is done. The caregiver washes her hands.

steps.title: Offer
steps.text: The caregiver sits comfortably with the child on her lap and offers RUTF from the packet, or on her finger.

steps.title: Encourage, never force
steps.text: She encourages the child gently all the time. If the child refuses she keeps quietly encouraging, and takes her time. The child must not be forced.

steps.title: Water
steps.text: Give plenty of water from a cup while the child takes the RUTF.

steps.title: Pass
steps.text: The child passes if he eats the amount in the table within 30 minutes.

read.text:
Weight of the childMinimum sachet (92 g) to eat in 30 minutesMaximum
Under 4 kg1/81/4
4 up to 6.9 kg1/41/3
7 up to 9.9 kg1/31/2
10 up to 14.9 kg1/23/4
15 kg and above3/41 or more
No appetite test is done if the child has a general danger sign, or pneumonia, persistent diarrhoea, dysentery, measles or malaria. If RUTF is not available for the test, refer.
Boniface weighs 9.9 kg and has a MUAC of 110 mm. What is the least RUTF he must eat to pass?
read.explanation: 7 up to 9.9 kg: at least 1/3 of a 92 g sachet.

stages.text: Noah has no oedema of both feet. He weighs 12.7 kg and stands to be measured: 104 cm. His MUAC is 116 mm. You explain each step to Rachel as you go.
stages.question: On the boys' height chart, the -3 line at 104 cm is 13.0 kg. What does Noah's weight tell you?
options: WFH below -3 z-score: a sign of SAM
stages.explanation: 12.7 kg is below the -3 line. His MUAC (116 mm) is above 115 mm, but one sign is enough.

stages.text: You check for medical complications. His cough is COUGH OR COLD, not pneumonia; he has no danger sign and no severe classification.
stages.question: What else do you do, as Noah is over 6 months?

stages.text: Noah weighs 12.7 kg, so he must eat at least 1/2 sachet in 30 minutes. Rachel washes her hands and gives RUTF from the packet with a cup of water, without forcing. After about 20 minutes Noah has eaten more than 1/2 sachet. He passed. You tell Rachel he has done well and need not eat more.

read.text: Classify a child as complicated or uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition, moderate acute malnutrition, or no acute malnutrition.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: There are four classifications for acute malnutrition. Read them in your chart booklet.

read.caption: Chart booklet: classify acute malnutrition (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

cards.back: Oedema of both feet, OR a SAM sign (WFH/L below -3 or MUAC below 115 mm) with a medical complication, or a breastfeeding problem under 6 months, or not able to finish the RUTF at 6 months or older. High risk of death from pneumonia, diarrhoea, measles and other severe diseases: refer urgently.
MUAC below 115 mm or WFH/L below -3, with no complication and the appetite test passed. Needs RUTF and oral antibiotics; at risk of death from serious disease.
MUAC 115 up to 125 mm, or WFH/L between -3 and -2, and no oedema. Higher risk of severe disease.
MUAC 125 mm or more, or WFH/L -2 or more, and no oedema. Under 2 years, assess feeding.

read.text: Sudan national booklet: Pre-referral treatment for COMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION: the first dose of antibiotic (oral amoxicillin if the child can take oral medicine, or IM ampicillin and gentamicin), treat to prevent low blood sugar, keep the child warm, refer urgently. UNCOMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION: oral amoxicillin for 5 days, refer to the outpatient therapeutic programme (OTP) and give RUTF if 6 months or older, assess feeding and counsel, follow up in 14 days. MODERATE ACUTE MALNUTRITION: refer to the supplementary feeding programme, assess feeding and counsel, follow up in 30 days. Feeding problem: follow up in 7 days. WHO module (page 27): Complicated SAM: first dose of amoxicillin, 50 ml of 10% glucose or sugar water, keep warm, refer. Uncomplicated SAM: oral antibiotics for 5 days, RUTF, assess for possible TB, follow up in 7 days. Moderate: assess feeding and counsel, assess for possible TB, follow up in 30 days (the text says 5 days if there is a feeding problem).
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: Classify each child.

items.text: MUAC 112 mm, no complications, passed the appetite test
WFH/L below -3 and failed the appetite test
MUAC 117 mm and no oedema
WFH/L between -1 and -2
WFH/L between -3 and -2
MUAC 113 mm and signs of shock
Under 6 months, WFL below -3, not breastfeeding effectively
Oedema of both feet
items.why: Oedema of both feet is always referred.

stages.text: Noah has one sign of SAM (WFH below -3), no oedema, no medical complication, and he passed the appetite test.
stages.question: How do you classify him?

stages.text: You look at the treatment column.
stages.question: Which treatments does Noah need for his malnutrition?
options: Oral amoxicillin for 5 days and RUTF from the OTP

sections.title: Treat severe acute malnutrition with RUTF

read.text: Give the right amount of RUTF for the child's weight, counsel the caregiver, and know when RUTF is stopped.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: A child with UNCOMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION must receive RUTF. RUTF is the only food that thin children need for their recovery. If the child is still breastfeeding, breastfeeding continues. RUTF is a treatment: it must be given in the correct quantity, by weight.

Weight (kg)Sachets (92 g) a daySachets a week
4.0 – 4.9214
5.0 – 6.92½18
7.0 – 8.4321
8.5 – 9.43½25
9.5 – 10.4428
10.5 – 11.94½32
12 and above535

Sudan national booklet: RUTF by weight from the national dose table: 10.5 up to 12 kg, 4½ sachets a day (32 a week); 12 kg and above, 5 sachets a day (35 a week). Noah (12.7 kg) gets 5 sachets a day, 35 a week. WHO module (page 32): The WHO table goes on: 10.5–14.9 kg, 4½ sachets a day (32 a week); 15–19.9 kg, 5 a day (35 a week); 20–29.9 kg, 6 a day (40 a week). WHO also gives paste amounts in grams. In the WHO module Noah gets 4½ sachets a day, 32 a week.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

cards.back: Wash hands before giving RUTF.
Sit with the child on the lap and gently offer RUTF. Encourage, without forced feeding.
Give small, regular meals of RUTF: 5 to 6 meals a day.
If still breastfeeding, continue, and offer breast milk first before every RUTF feed.
Offer plenty of clean water to drink from a cup when the child eats RUTF.
RUTF is a special food for thin children only. It should not be shared with the family.

read.text: When is RUTF stopped?

RUTF is given until the weight-for-height is above -2 z-score for 2 consecutive visits, OR the child has gained 15% weight, and the child is well and alert. A child with oedema loses weight as the swelling goes down; RUTF is not stopped until the weight gain above is reached AND the oedema has been gone for at least 2 weeks.
Sheena's weight has changed from 32.5 kg to 38.0 kg on RUTF. Should she stop?
options: Yes: she has gained more than 15%
read.explanation: 15% of 32.5 kg is about 4.9 kg; she gained 5.5 kg.

read.text: Rakim's weight has changed from 20.5 kg to 23 kg. Should he stop?
read.explanation: 15% of 20.5 kg is about 3.1 kg; he gained 2.5 kg.

read.text: Treat SOME DEHYDRATION in a child with severe acute malnutrition with ReSoMal, not normal ORS.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: A child with severe acute malnutrition and dehydration is managed differently. A child with SEVERE DEHYDRATION is referred urgently. A child with SOME DEHYDRATION can be treated in the health facility, but NOT with normal ORS: normal ORS has high sodium and low potassium, which does not suit a severely malnourished child.

steps.title: Preferred: ReSoMal
steps.text: 5 ml/kg every 30 minutes for the first 2 hours, then 5–10 ml/kg per hour for the next 4–10 hours, on alternate hours with RUTF.

steps.title: No ReSoMal: half-strength ORS
steps.text: Prepare half-strength ORS with concentrated electrolyte/mineral solution, in the same doses.

steps.title: Neither available
steps.text: Refer urgently to the nearest hospital.

read.text: The child is not sent home before improvement is seen. Assess every 30 minutes for the first 2 hours, then every hour for the next 4–10 hours. If the child improves, send the caregiver home with ReSoMal or half-strength ORS for two days: 50–100 ml after each loose stool. She returns urgently if the child does not improve, and for follow-up after two days. If the child gets worse or does not improve, refer urgently.
Lisa has SOME DEHYDRATION and SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION. What do you do now?
options: Give ORS and zinc as in the diarrhoea chart
Send her home with half-strength ORS and RUTF
read.explanation: She is treated in the facility, and goes home only once she improves.

read.text: Look for palmar pallor and classify a child as severe anaemia, anaemia, or no anaemia.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Anaemia is a reduced number of red cells, or a reduced amount of haemoglobin in each red cell. Iron deficiency is the most common cause; folate, vitamin B12 and vitamin A deficiency are others. A child can also become anaemic from:

• Parasites such as hookworm or whipworm, which cause blood loss from the gut
  • Malaria, which destroys red cells quickly; repeated or badly treated malaria can cause slow-developing anaemia. Anaemia is often due to both malnutrition and malaria.
Look for palmar pallor

Pallor is unusual paleness of the skin, a sign of anaemia. Look at the skin of the child's palm. Hold the palm open by grasping it gently from the side. Do not stretch the fingers backwards: this can cause pallor by blocking the blood supply. Compare the colour with your own palm and with other children's palms.

cards.back: The skin of the palm is pale.
The skin of the palm is very pale, or so pale that it looks white.

read.caption: Chart booklet: anaemia (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

cards.back: Severe palmar pallor. Refer urgently.
Some palmar pallor. Give iron (not if the child is on RUTF), give mebendazole, assess feeding, follow up in 14 days.
No palmar pallor. Under 2 years, assess feeding and counsel.

read.text: Sudan national booklet: ANAEMIA: give iron for 14 days, but not if sickle cell anaemia is known or suspected or the child is on RUTF; mebendazole if 1 year or older with no dose in the last 6 months; assess feeding and counsel; follow up in 14 days. The national anaemia box has no malaria-risk step: every child with fever has a malaria test in the fever assessment. WHO module (page 36): In a high malaria risk area, do a malaria test when there is some pallor, and give an oral antimalarial if it is positive (even without fever). If no test is available in a high risk area, give an oral antimalarial.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.title: Demonstration: assess malnutrition and anaemia
read.caption: WHO course DVD, disc 2: "Assess for malnutrition, anaemia and ear problems". It also covers feeding problems, which you will learn in the well child module.

stages.text: You take Noah's hand and look at his palm, and Rachel puts her hand out to compare. Noah's palms are quite a bit paler than his mother's. They are pale, but not white.
stages.question: How do you classify Noah?
stages.explanation: Some palmar pallor. If his palms were white, it would be SEVERE ANAEMIA.

stages.text: Noah's form now shows: COUGH OR COLD, UNCOMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION and ANAEMIA.

read.text: Give iron by age or weight, give mebendazole, and counsel the caregiver about iron at home.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Iron

A child with some palmar pallor needs iron. Do not give iron to a child receiving RUTF: RUTF has enough iron and folic acid to treat mild anaemia. Give the caregiver enough iron for 14 days: one dose daily, and return for more iron in 14 days.

Age or weightFerrous sulphate 200 mg + folate tabletFerrous fumarate syrup 100 mg/5 mlIron polymaltose syrup 50 mg/5 ml
2 up to 4 months (4 – <6 kg)1 ml2 ml
4 up to 12 months (6 – <10 kg)1.25 ml2.5 ml
12 months up to 3 years (10 – <14 kg)½ tablet2 ml4 ml
3 up to 5 years (14 – <20 kg)½ tablet2.5 ml5 ml

Sudan national booklet: The national dose table adds iron polymaltose syrup (50 mg/5 ml) and says not to give iron when sickle cell anaemia is known or suspected. WHO module (page 41): The WHO table gives ferrous sulphate tablets and ferrous fumarate syrup only.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

cards.back: One dose daily for 14 days, then come back for more.
Iron may make the stools black. This is expected; do not stop the iron.
Keep iron out of the child's reach. An overdose of iron can be fatal or make the child very ill.

read.text: Mebendazole
Hookworm and whipworm cause iron loss through bleeding in the gut. A child with anaemia who is 1 year or older and has not had mebendazole in the last 6 months is given mebendazole.

Sudan national booklet: Mebendazole syrup 100 mg/5 ml: 5 ml morning and evening for 3 days, and repeat the course after 2 weeks (1 year or older). WHO module (page 41): 500 mg as a single dose in the clinic (one 500 mg tablet or five 100 mg tablets). The WHO chart says 2 years or older; the text says 1 year or older.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

stages.text: Noah has COUGH OR COLD, UNCOMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION and ANAEMIA, and has had no mebendazole in the last 6 months.
stages.question: Which treatments do you identify?
options: Cough remedy, oral amoxicillin, RUTF, mebendazole
stages.explanation: No iron: Noah is taking RUTF.

stages.text: You start oral amoxicillin today for 5 days. Noah weighs 12.7 kg, so he gets 5 sachets of RUTF a day, 35 for the week. You give mebendazole. You explain to Rachel that his cough is not severe, and that getting Noah to a healthier weight is very important to protect him from serious disease. She looks frightened, and you reassure her that RUTF and some changes to his diet should help.

read.text: Counsel a caregiver on several home treatments, teach with the three steps, and check understanding.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Five topics to counsel Rachel on today

steps.title: 1. Cough
steps.text: Home care, with a safe local remedy to soothe the throat.

steps.title: 2. Oral amoxicillin
steps.text: The dose and schedule for 5 days.

steps.title: 3. RUTF at home
steps.text: The amount, schedule and how to give it: clean hands, on the lap, gently without forcing, small meals 5 to 6 times a day, water from a cup, not shared.

steps.title: 4. Feeding
steps.text: Feeding recommendations for his age (you will learn them in the well child module).

steps.title: 5. When to return
steps.text: The signs to return immediately, including if Noah does not eat RUTF, and the follow-up visit.

read.text: Use the 3 basic teaching steps: give information, demonstrate, and let Rachel practise. Show her how to give RUTF from the sachet, with water in a cup.

Checking questions

  • How will you prepare a safe cough remedy at home?
  • How will you give the RUTF to Noah?
  • What are important things to remember about giving RUTF at home?
  • What foods can you give Noah? Can you give me an example of one day's feeding?
  • When will you come back to the clinic with Noah?
How can "Will you give your child more nutritious foods?" be asked as a checking question?
options: What foods will you give your child so that he gets more of the vitamins his body needs?
Do you have nutritious foods at home?
Do you understand the recommendations I just gave you?
read.explanation: A good checking question cannot be answered with yes or no.

stages.text: Rachel is a little confused when she explains how to give RUTF, but she remembers the tips, especially not giving RUTF to others in the house.
stages.question: What do you do?
options: Explain again, demonstrate, let her practise, and ask again
Give her the sachets and let her go
stages.explanation: After a second round, you are satisfied with her answers.

stages.text: Rachel worries she will forget something, because Noah has many treatments. You give her a written dose schedule. You tell her she is a good mother for noticing Noah's illness and bringing him, and that the treatments should help him.

read.text: Follow up a child with severe or moderate acute malnutrition, anaemia or a feeding problem.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Sudan national booklet: Follow-up times in the national booklet: UNCOMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION, 14 days (the OTP gives RUTF at its own visits); MODERATE ACUTE MALNUTRITION, 30 days; ANAEMIA, 14 days; a feeding problem, 7 days. WHO module (page 44): Uncomplicated SAM receiving RUTF: every week. Feeding problem: 5 days. Moderate acute malnutrition: 14 days in the follow-up section (30 days in the classification table).
read.label: Sudan national protocol

cards.back: Give iron for 14 more days, and ask the caregiver to come back in 14 days.
Keep giving iron every 14 days for 2 months.
Refer the child for assessment.

read.title: Each follow-up visit for SAM on RUTF

steps.title: Measure
steps.text: Weight and MUAC at each visit, height every 4 weeks; WFH z-score at every visit.

steps.title: Look
steps.text: Oedema of both feet; temperature, pulse, breathing rate and a medical check.

steps.title: Appetite
steps.text: Appetite test with RUTF.

steps.title: Supply and counsel
steps.text: Give the RUTF ration and review the counselling messages.

cards.back: MUAC and/or WFH have improved. Praise the caregiver. Continue RUTF until WFH is above -2 or the child has gained 15%.
A home visit may show problems with care or sharing of food. Ask the caregiver to come back. After one month with no response, refer for medical review and tests for an underlying illness.
Refer to hospital or a feeding programme.

read.text:
Common reasons a child does not respond

  • Quality of treatment: missed medical complication, poor appetite test, poor home-care instructions, wrong amount of RUTF, routine medicines not given, a facility far from home
  • Home or child: few visits, RUTF shared or too little, medicines not taken, sharing of family food, micronutrient deficiency, malabsorption, psychological trauma, infection or underlying disease, an unwilling caregiver
A child can be discharged from outpatient treatment when there has been no oedema for at least 2 weeks, AND the child has gained 15% or has been above -2 z-score for two consecutive visits.
read.label: Remember

stages.text: Rachel brings Noah back as agreed. Noah has no new symptoms and his cough has cleared. He now weighs 13 kg, still 104 cm. His MUAC is 117 mm. On the chart, 13.0 kg at 104 cm is on the -3 line.
stages.question: Do you stop RUTF?
options: Yes: he is no longer below -3
stages.explanation: He has improved, but RUTF stops only when he is above -2 for 2 consecutive visits or has gained 15%.

stages.text: His palms look improved, and you reclassify NO ANAEMIA. You give new RUTF supplies, and ask Rachel to explain and show how she gives it: you are pleased. You talk about the foods she gave in the past week, and other options for any that were too expensive or not available. Rachel hoped Noah would be better by now; you explain that gaining weight takes time and a lot of nutrition, and praise her progress.

sections.title: Using this module in your clinic

read.text: Plan how to practise the skills of this module in your own clinic.
read.label: In this lesson

cards.back: What causes malnutrition in your area? Does it change by season or region? Check every child: oedema of both feet, WFH/L z-score, MUAC; complications and the appetite test if SAM; palmar pallor. Classify with your chart booklet.

Prevent low blood sugar before referral; give RUTF; give iron and mebendazole. Find the nutrition resources in your area: nutrition counselling, OTP and supplementary feeding programmes, and food support.
Counsel on giving RUTF safely at home and on feeding recommendations. Use clinic materials to teach about food.
Use the IMNCI follow-up instructions for malnutrition and anaemia.

read.text: Ear problems are a common reason for coming to the clinic. You check all children for ear problems.

steps.title: For ALL sick children
steps.text: Ask about the child's problems, check for general danger signs, and assess cough, diarrhoea and fever.

steps.title: Then ASK: does the child have an ear problem?
steps.text: If NO, go on. If YES, assess and classify with the colour-coded ear chart.

steps.title: Continue the assessment
steps.text: Check for malnutrition and anaemia, immunization status and other problems.

read.text: What you will be able to do

After you study this module, you will be able to:

  • Explain why it is necessary to check all children for ear problems
  • Explain why ear problems can cause long-term ear damage and deafness
  • Recognize tender swelling behind the ear, the clinical sign of mastoiditis
  • Decide whether an ear infection is acute or chronic
  • Classify ear problems using the IMNCI charts
  • Counsel caregivers on drying an ear by wicking
  • Follow up a child with an ear problem
Which part of the recording form is used in this module?

read.caption: The national recording form: ear problem

read.text: Before you begin
What do you know now about managing ear problems? Check quickly with five questions. After the module you will answer the same questions, and see what you have learned.
Start the visit of a child with fever and ear pain, and assess the main symptoms before the ear.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Ear problems
read.caption: Watch this first.

read.text: You will follow Telisa and her mother Sara through the module.

stages.text: Sara and her daughter Telisa live some distance from the clinic; they came by taxi and on foot. Telisa is small and looks very tired. Sara puts her on her lap and holds a wet cloth on her neck: she says Telisa has been feeling hot.

Telisa is 3 years old and weighs 13 kg. Her temperature is 37.5 °C. She has felt hot for 3 days, and for the past 2 nights she woke complaining of ear pain. You praise Sara for bringing her. Telisa drinks with no trouble, is not vomiting and has had no convulsions. She sits on Sara's lap, holding her mother's arm and looking around the room.
stages.question: Does Telisa have a general danger sign?

stages.text: Telisa has no cough and no diarrhoea. She has fever: 37.5 °C and feels hot. She bends her neck easily to look at her mother's shoes, so there is no stiff neck. She has no runny nose, rash or red eyes, and no measles in the last 3 months. Her malaria test is negative.
stages.question: How do you classify Telisa's fever?
stages.explanation: No danger sign, no stiff neck, negative test.

stages.text: Now you will check Telisa for the next main symptom: an ear problem. You check every child for an ear problem.

read.text: Explain how an ear infection can cause deafness, and when it becomes a severe disease.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Ear infections rarely cause death, but they cause many days of illness. They are the main cause of deafness in developing countries, and deafness causes learning problems at school. Assessing, classifying and treating ear problems prevents pain now, and more serious consequences later.

steps.title: Pus behind the eardrum
steps.text: Pus collects behind the eardrum and causes pain, and often fever.

steps.title: The eardrum bursts
steps.text: If the infection is not treated, the eardrum may burst. The pus discharges and the pain lessens; the fever may stop, but the child hears poorly because the eardrum has a hole.

steps.title: Heals, or keeps draining
steps.text: Usually the eardrum heals by itself. Sometimes the discharge continues, the eardrum does not heal, and the child becomes deaf in that ear.

read.title: When an ear problem becomes a severe disease

cards.back: The infection spreads to the bone behind the ear (the mastoid). Urgent referral.
The infection spreads from the ear to the brain. Urgent referral.

read.text: Why are ear problems important in IMNCI?
options: They are common, and can cause deafness and serious infection
They are a major killer of children
They are always a sign of brain infection

read.text: Ask about ear pain and discharge, look for pus and feel for tender swelling behind the ear.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Ask about an ear problem for ALL sick children. If the caregiver says NO, go on to malnutrition and anaemia. If YES, ask, look and feel.

read.caption: Chart booklet: ear problem (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

cards.back: Ear pain can mean an ear infection. If the caregiver is not sure, ask if the child has been irritable and rubbing the ear.

cards.front: ASK: ear discharge? For how long?
cards.back: Use words the caregiver understands, and give her time to remember when it started. Discharge for 14 days or more is treated as chronic; less than 14 days as acute.

cards.front: LOOK: pus draining from the ear?
cards.back: Look inside the ear. Draining pus is a sign of infection, even if the child has no pain.

cards.front: FEEL: tender swelling behind the ear?
cards.back: Feel behind both ears and compare. Tenderness AND swelling may be mastoiditis, a deep infection of the mastoid bone. In infants the swelling may be above the ear. Do not confuse it with swollen lymph nodes.

read.text: The mother says the child has no ear problem. What do you do?
Classify a child as mastoiditis, acute ear infection, chronic ear infection or no ear infection, and classify Telisa.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: There are four classifications for an ear problem. In order of seriousness:

read.caption: Chart booklet: classify ear problem (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

cards.back: Tender swelling behind the ear. Refer urgently; the child may need injectable antibiotics or surgery.
Pus seen draining from the ear and discharge for less than 14 days, OR ear pain.
Pus seen draining from the ear and discharge for 14 days or more.
No ear pain and no pus seen draining from the ear.

read.text: Ear pain counts when it wakes the child at night, the child tells you the ear hurts, or the child is or was distressed with pain. If the only history is scratching or pulling the ear and the child does not seem in pain, do not classify ear pain: children often rub their ears.

An infant who is irritable and slightly feverish may have an ear infection without being able to show where it hurts. The fever has no obvious cause, so ask the caregiver to bring the child back if there is no improvement: by then pus may be draining.
Classify each child.

items.text: Pus draining from Ben's ear for about 3 months
Leboheng cannot sleep because his ears hurt; discharge for less than 1 week
Akiiki has fever, swelling behind her ear, and cries when you touch it
Khotso wakes at night crying because his right ear hurts
Jamie says his ears hurt but does not wake at night; no discharge
items.why: Pain that does not wake him, and no pus.

stages.text: Telisa cried most of the night because her ear hurt. Sara says there has been discharge on and off for about a year. You look, and see no pus draining. You feel behind her ears, and find tender swelling behind one ear.
stages.question: How do you classify?
stages.explanation: Tender swelling behind the ear is MASTOIDITIS, the most serious classification.

sections.title: Treat an ear problem, and refer Telisa

read.text: Give the treatments for each ear classification, and prepare a child with mastoiditis for referral.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Sudan national booklet: MASTOIDITIS: first dose of antibiotic (oral amoxicillin if the child can take oral medicine, or IM ampicillin and gentamicin), first dose of paracetamol for pain, refer urgently. ACUTE EAR INFECTION: oral amoxicillin for 5 days, paracetamol for pain, dry the ear by wicking, follow up in 5 days. CHRONIC EAR INFECTION: dry the ear by wicking, then ciprofloxacin ear drops 3 times daily for 14 days, follow up in 5 days. Refer for assessment if there is a hearing problem. WHO module (page 17): Mastoiditis: first dose of an appropriate antibiotic (the text names IM ceftriaxone) and paracetamol, refer. Chronic ear infection: wicking and topical quinolone ear drops for 14 days (the text says no antibiotic, and acetic acid drops if available).
read.label: Sudan national protocol

cards.back: The antibiotics that treat pneumonia also work against the bacteria that cause most acute ear infections.
Relieves ear pain (or high fever, 38.5 °C or above).

cards.front: No oral antibiotic for chronic infection
cards.back: The bacteria of chronic ear infection are different. The most important and effective treatment is keeping the ear dry by wicking; the drops are put in after wicking, whenever pus is seen.

stages.text: Telisa has MASTOIDITIS, a red classification.
stages.question: What do you give before she leaves?
options: The first dose of antibiotic and the first dose of paracetamol

stages.text: You write a referral note. Sara is confused: all children have fevers and ear problems, and her husband thinks ear pain goes away by itself. Telisa is moving around fine.
stages.question: How do you respond first?
options: Agree that ear problems are common, and explain that Telisa's infection is now outside the ear, in the bone

stages.text: Sara is still unsure. You explain that untreated, the infection could damage Telisa's hearing, or spread to her brain; her fever is her body fighting the infection. Sara looks afraid. You tell her not to be afraid: you explain so she understands. You are firm: if she goes to the hospital now, they can treat the infection.

sections.title: Counsel: dry the ear by wicking

read.text: Teach a caregiver to wick an ear dry, with the three teaching steps and checking questions.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Counsel with ASK, PRAISE, ADVISE, CHECK

cards.back: Find out what the caregiver is already doing for the child.
Praise what she has done well. Never be judgemental.
Advise how to treat the child at home, with the teaching steps.
Check her understanding with checking questions.

steps.title: 1. Give information
steps.text: How to give the treatment, how much, for how long, and why it is important.

steps.title: 2. Show an example
steps.text: For example, how to hold the child still and wick the ear.

steps.title: 3. Let her practise
steps.text: She wicks the child's ear while you watch: the most important part of teaching a task.

read.title: How to wick an ear dry

steps.title: Make a wick
steps.text: Use clean, absorbent cotton cloth or soft, strong tissue paper (clinic paper towels are suitable). Do not use a cotton-tipped applicator, a stick, or flimsy paper that falls apart in the ear.

steps.title: Wick
steps.text: Clean the ear with the wick, then place a clean wick in the ear until it is wet.

steps.title: Replace
steps.text: Replace the wet wick with a clean one.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Repeat until the wick stays dry. Then the ear is dry.

read.text:
Tell the caregiver

  • Wick the ear dry 3 times daily, for as many days as it takes until the wick no longer gets wet and no pus drains.
  • Do not put anything (oil, fluid or anything else) in the ear between wickings, except the recommended ear drops.
  • Do not plug the ear: it needs air to dry. Do not let the child go swimming; no water should get in the ear.

Sudan national booklet: For CHRONIC EAR INFECTION, after wicking give ciprofloxacin ear drops 3 times daily for 14 days. WHO module (page 20): Recommended drops (1% acetic acid) are used if available; if not, nothing is put in the ear.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text:
Checking questions

  • What materials will you use to make the wick at home?
  • How many times a day will you dry the ear with a wick?
  • What else will you put in your child's ear?
Is this good wicking advice?

items.text: Use a stiff piece of newspaper as a wick
items.why: Use soft, absorbent cloth or tissue.

items.text: Wick 3 times a day until the wick stays dry
Plug the ear with cotton between wickings
items.why: The ear needs air to dry.

items.text: Put warm oil in the ear at night
items.why: Nothing goes in the ear except the recommended drops.

items.text: Keep the child from swimming

read.text: Use five skills that help a caregiver feel confident: accept, praise, inform, use simple words, and suggest.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: A caregiver who feels confident, informed and supported cares better for her child, gives treatment better and feeds better. These skills help.

cards.front: 1. Accept how she thinks and feels
cards.back: Do not disagree, and do not agree with a mistaken idea: respond neutrally. "My milk is weak and thin": not "Oh no, milk is never weak", not "Yes, thin milk can be a problem", but "I see, you are worried about your milk."
Look for good practices and praise them. It builds confidence, encourages her to continue, and makes it easier to accept suggestions later.
One or two pieces at a time, relevant to her situation now, said in a positive way. Wait to correct a mistaken idea until you have accepted and praised.
Not technical terms. "Every time your baby suckles, your breast makes more milk."
Avoid always, never, must, should. Try: "Have you considered...?", "Would it be possible...?", "What about trying...?"

read.text: A caregiver says: "My baby has a cold and a blocked nose and just cries all the time." Which response accepts how she feels?
options: You are upset about him, aren't you?
Don't worry, your baby is doing very well.

read.text: A baby is exclusively breastfed. He gained some weight last month, but his growth line is rising too slowly. Which remark builds the mother's confidence?
options: Your baby gained weight last month just on your breast milk
Your baby's growth line is going up too slowly
I don't think your baby is gaining enough weight

read.text: Which is a suggestion, not a command?
options: You may wish to try feeding him with a cup.
Use a cup to feed your baby.

read.text: Reassess a child with an ear infection at follow-up and decide what to do.

read.text: Sudan national booklet: Follow up ACUTE and CHRONIC EAR INFECTION in 5 days. WHO module (page 27): Acute ear infection: 5 days if discharge persists, otherwise 14 days. Chronic ear infection: 14 days.

read.text: At the follow-up visit, reassess the ear problem and check for fever. Then choose the treatment from the child's signs.
Tender swelling behind the ear, or high fever (38.5 °C or above), means the child has become worse: refer URGENTLY.
read.label: Remember

cards.back: Praise the caregiver. She comes back immediately if the ear becomes painful or discharges again.

Give 5 more days of the same antibiotic. Continue wicking if there is discharge. Ask her to show how she wicks, how often, and what problems she has; correct and encourage. Explain that drying is the only effective treatment of a draining ear, and that hearing loss can follow if it is not wicked. See the child again to make sure mastoiditis has not developed.

cards.front: Still discharging after 2 weeks of good wicking
cards.back: Refer.
Praise the caregiver, and advise when to return immediately.
Check that she wicks correctly, and explain why it matters.

cards.front: No improvement despite drops and good wicking
cards.back: Persistent pain, offensive discharge or reduced hearing: refer.

read.text: This module shows how IMNCI helps to give HIV care, treatment, support and prevention to children. Worldwide, 3.4 million children were living with HIV in 2011. Children with suspected or confirmed HIV infection have special needs, so they are cared for differently from children who are not infected.

What do you know now about HIV care for children? Check quickly with six questions. After the module you will answer the same questions, and see what you have learned.
Explain in simple words what the immune system, CD4 cells and opportunistic infections are.

read.title: HIV and the immune system
read.caption: Watch this first.

read.text: Every healthy person has a strong system to defend the body against disease: the immune system. White blood cells are an important part of it. They can be thought of as the "soldiers" of the body.

read.title: What HIV does in the body

steps.title: CD4 cells warn the body
steps.text: Some white blood cells (lymphocytes) have a marker called CD4. These CD4 cells warn the immune system that germs are trying to invade the body.

steps.title: HIV takes over CD4 cells
steps.text: HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) infects cells of the immune system; its main target is the CD4 cell. It hides its material in the nucleus, so the cell makes new copies of the virus.

steps.title: The cells die
steps.text: An infected CD4 cell makes many new copies of HIV, then dies. The copies infect other CD4 cells, and this goes on and on.

steps.title: The defence becomes weak
steps.text: With fewer CD4 cells the immune system becomes weaker, and germs that would not normally cause illness now do.

read.title: Three words to explain to a caregiver

cards.back: The immune system protects the body against infections.
CD4 cells are white blood cells that warn the immune system that germs are trying to invade the body. The CD4 count shows how well the body's defence is still working.
An infection that cannot attack a healthy body, but takes the opportunity when the immune system is weak. Examples are oral thrush and herpes zoster.

read.text: Children are different from adults

In adults it usually takes 7 to 10 years after infection before serious illness. HIV progresses much more rapidly in children, because their immune system is not yet well developed, especially if they were infected in the womb or at delivery.

As the damage gets worse, children become highly vulnerable to life-threatening illnesses such as PCP pneumonia, lymphoma, recurrent bacterial infections and HIV brain damage (encephalopathy). These are called AIDS-defining diseases. As HIV disease progresses, the CD4 count or percentage falls.
Why must HIV be found early in a child?
options: HIV damages a child's immune system much faster than an adult's
Children always show wasting first, like adults
read.explanation: Children progress from HIV to AIDS much more rapidly than adults, and may become severely ill very quickly.

read.text: Explain how mother-to-child transmission happens, how big the risk is, and what HIV exposed means.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.text: Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT), also called vertical transmission, is the main way young children are infected. Other ways are sexual abuse, unsafe injections, and transfusion of infected blood. Not all HIV-infected women pass the virus to their child.

read.title: Three times when HIV can pass from mother to child

steps.title: Pregnancy
steps.text: The risk is low, because the placenta protects the baby.

steps.title: Labour and delivery
steps.text: The risk increases: the baby can suck, absorb or aspirate blood or cervical fluid.

steps.title: Breastfeeding
steps.text: HIV can pass in breast milk. Mixed feeding carries a higher risk than exclusive breastfeeding, because other foods and fluids can damage the lining of the baby's gut.

read.text:
If 20 HIV-infected women have babies with no interventionBabies
Infected during pregnancy, labour or deliveryabout 4 (20%)
Infected during breastfeedingabout 3 (15%)
Not infectedabout 13
Overall risk of MTCTabout 7 of 20 (35%)
This risk is lower when the mother or child receives ARV prophylaxis.
The term mother-to-child transmission does not imply blame. A woman can acquire HIV from an infected partner, or from contaminated blood or instruments, often without knowing it.
read.label: Remember

read.text: HIV EXPOSED: an infant born to a woman known to be HIV-infected. The infant cannot be called HIV-positive or HIV-negative until an appropriate HIV test confirms the status.
read.label: Key point

read.text: Without treatment

If untreated, three-quarters of children infected through MTCT die before the age of 5. Without ART or cotrimoxazole, about one third die by 1 year and half by 2 years, many at home before they ever reach a health facility.

read.title: Three ways to prevent these deaths

cards.back: Early diagnosis of HIV.
Starting antiretroviral therapy (ART).
Other prophylaxis and treatments, such as cotrimoxazole.

read.text: Twenty HIV-infected women deliver with no intervention and breastfeed. About how many babies will be infected?
read.explanation: About 7 of 20 (35%): about 4 in pregnancy or delivery and about 3 through breastfeeding.

read.text: You will follow Peter and his mother Lungile through this module, from his first visit to his care on ART.

stages.text: Peter is 6 months old. His mother Lungile brings him because he has had a cough for 3 days. He weighs 7.2 kg and his temperature is 37.5 °C. He has no general danger signs.
Peter breathes 54 times a minute. He has no chest indrawing, no stridor and no wheeze.
stages.question: How do you classify Peter's cough?
options: SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE
stages.explanation: At 2 up to 12 months, fast breathing is 50 breaths per minute or more. Fast breathing with no chest indrawing or stridor is PNEUMONIA.

stages.text: Peter has no diarrhoea and no ear problem, and he is not low weight for age. Lungile is worried: she was recently told she has HIV, and she is receiving care at another clinic. She is breastfeeding Peter.
stages.question: What does Lungile's HIV status tell you about Peter?
options: He is HIV exposed: his own status is not yet known
He cannot be infected because he looks well
stages.explanation: A child born to an HIV-infected mother is HIV exposed until a test confirms his status.

read.caption: The national chart booklet: classify cough or difficult breathing

read.text: In the next lessons you will learn about HIV tests, and how to assess and classify Peter for HIV.
Say who should be tested for HIV, and what a serological and a virological (PCR) test detect.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. read.text: Who should be tested?

• All children born to an HIV-infected mother
  • All children with no known test result, whose mother's status you do not know
  • In a high HIV setting, every sick child

Serological tests (including rapid tests)Virological tests (DNA or RNA PCR)
What they detectAntibodies made by immune cells in response to HIV, not the virus itselfThe HIV virus itself, or products of the virus, in the blood
How to read themA mother's antibodies pass to her child. Most are gone by 12 months, but some remain until 18 months, so a positive test under 18 months does not show that the child is infected.A positive test reliably shows HIV infection at any age. A negative test in a child who has been breastfeeding does not rule out infection: test again 6 weeks or more after breastfeeding has completely stopped.

cards.back: Use a serological test. A positive test (with a confirmatory test) shows the child is HIV-infected.
A virological (PCR) test is the only reliable way to find the child's status. Test from 4 to 6 weeks of age.

read.text: Is this true of a serological test or a virological (PCR) test?

items.text: Detects antibodies to HIV
Detects the virus itself
A positive result may be the mother's antibodies in a child under 18 months
A positive result shows infection even in a 2-month-old
Rapid tests are this kind

sections.title: Read a test result under 18 months

read.text: Interpret an HIV test in a child under 18 months, using the child's breastfeeding status.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: For a child under 18 months, what a result means depends on the test, and on whether the child is still breastfeeding.

read.title: If a virological (PCR) test is available (test from 4 to 6 weeks)

cards.back: The child is infected: the test finds the virus itself.
The child is not infected now, but could still become infected while breastfeeding.

read.title: If only a serological test is available

cards.back: The child has been exposed to HIV, but may or may not be infected. All HIV-exposed infants should have a virological test.
Usually the child is not infected, as long as the child has not breastfed in the last 6 weeks.

read.text:
Serological test, child under 18 monthsPOSITIVENEGATIVE
Not breastfeeding, and not in the last 6 weeksHIV exposed and/or infected: manage as if infected. Repeat the test at 18 months.HIV negative: the child is not infected.
BreastfeedingHIV exposed and/or infected: manage as if infected. Repeat at 18 months, or once breastfeeding has stopped for more than 6 weeks.The child can still be infected by breastfeeding. Repeat once breastfeeding has stopped for more than 6 weeks.
Breastfeeding matters. A test can only show that a child is not infected once the child has stopped breastfeeding for at least 6 weeks.
read.label: Key point

read.title: The early infant diagnosis algorithm, in short

steps.title: HIV-exposed infant under 18 months
steps.text: Do a virological test (for a newborn, at birth or at the first postnatal visit, usually 4 to 6 weeks).

steps.title: Positive
steps.text: The infant is likely infected. Start ART without delay, and repeat the virological test to confirm.

steps.title: Negative, never breastfed
steps.text: The infant is not infected.

steps.title: Negative, breastfed
steps.text: The infant stays at risk until breastfeeding stops completely. Monitor regularly.

steps.title: Well at 9 months
steps.text: Do an antibody test at about 9 months. If positive, do a virological test. Repeat the antibody test at 18 months and/or 6 weeks after breastfeeding stops.

steps.title: Signs suggestive of HIV at any time
steps.text: Test. If no virological test is available, assume the child is infected if sick.

sections.title: Counsel a mother about testing her child

read.text: Explain to a mother why her child needs an HIV test, and what to do if she refuses.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.

read.text: Many mothers, and even health workers, are reluctant to discuss HIV. But the problem will not be solved while there is secrecy. The mother of a child classified HIV EXPOSED needs counselling about an HIV test for her child.

steps.title: Explain why
steps.text: Explain why it is important to test the child, for example because the status is unknown.

steps.title: Explain the benefit
steps.text: Testing lets the child get care that improves life: antibiotics to prevent infections, vitamin supplements, growth monitoring, treatment of illness, ART if needed, and feeding counselling under about 2 years.

steps.title: Listen
steps.text: Let the mother ask questions, and address her concerns. If she agrees, arrange the test in the normal way.

steps.title: Think of the family
steps.text: Since most children are infected by their mother, you may need to discuss testing her and her partner, perhaps even before testing the child.

steps.title: After the test
steps.text: Make an appointment for the result and post-test counselling. After a rapid test, counsel straight away if the mother agrees. Keep privacy and confidentiality.

read.text: HIV can bring feelings of guilt, fear of rejection, and fear of revealing the mother's own status and how she was infected.
A mother does not want her child tested. What do you do?
read.answer: Listen to and address her concerns and reasons. You are an advocate for the child: negotiate in the child's best interest, and reassure her about the treatment, care and support the child can have once diagnosed. It may help for her to talk without the child present.

read.text: When is post-test counselling done after a rapid (serological) test?
options: Straight away, if the mother agrees
Only if the result is positive

read.text: Ask about HIV tests and feeding, and classify a child's HIV status with the colour-coded chart.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. read.title: Classify HIV status
read.caption: Watch this first.

read.text: For ALL sick children, after checking for malnutrition and anaemia, ask: has the child or mother been tested for HIV? Use this chart if the child is not already enrolled in HIV care.

steps.title: ASK: has the mother and/or child had an HIV test?
steps.text: If YES, note the mother's status (positive or negative) and the child's virological and serological results. A mother who tested negative long ago could be infected now: the more recent the test, the more accurate.

steps.title: If NO test result
steps.text: Test the mother. If she is positive, test the child: a serological test from 18 months, a virological test under 18 months.

steps.title: If the mother is positive and the child negative or untested
steps.text: ASK: was the child breastfeeding at the time of the test or in the 6 weeks before it? Is the child breastfeeding now? If yes, are the mother and child on ARV prophylaxis?

read.text:
SignsClassify asTreatment
Positive virological test in the child, OR positive serological test in a child 18 months or olderCONFIRMED HIV INFECTION (yellow)Give cotrimoxazole prophylaxis. Give HIV care and start ART. Assess feeding and counsel. Advise on home care. Refer for TB assessment and INH preventive therapy. Follow up regularly.
Mother positive AND child's virological test negative while breastfeeding or less than 6 weeks after stopping, OR mother positive and child not yet tested, OR positive serological test in a child under 18 monthsHIV EXPOSED (yellow)Give cotrimoxazole prophylaxis. Start or continue ARV prophylaxis as recommended. Do a virological test to confirm. Assess feeding and counsel. Advise on home care. Follow up regularly.
Negative HIV test in the mother or childHIV INFECTION UNLIKELY (green)Treat, counsel and follow up existing infections.

If the status of the mother or child is unknown, offer testing, especially if the child has malnutrition, pneumonia, diarrhoea, chronic cough or other signs that suggest HIV. This is provider-initiated testing and counselling.
read.label: Remember

stages.text: Lungile tested positive for HIV. She did not receive ART prophylaxis for PMTCT. Peter is still breastfeeding and has never been tested. You counsel Lungile, and do a serological test. It is positive.
stages.question: How do you classify Peter?
stages.explanation: Peter is 6 months old: a positive serological test under 18 months may be Lungile's antibodies. He is HIV EXPOSED. His status can only be confirmed with a virological test, at least 6 weeks after he stops breastfeeding.

stages.text: With the classification HIV EXPOSED, Peter will be followed up every month.

sections.title: Assess and classify a young infant for HIV

read.text: Explain why a young infant is classified only by test results, and classify young infants.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Young infants with HIV usually have no signs directly related to HIV. They do get ill, but with common illnesses such as pneumonia or diarrhoea. So the assessment and classification of a young infant uses HIV test results only.

Young infants with HIV may look well, but can become ill and die very quickly. All infants born to HIV-infected mothers should have a virological test, and the result must come back to the clinic and to the caregiver.
read.label: Key point

steps.text: After possible bacterial infection, jaundice and diarrhoea, ASK: has the mother and/or young infant had an HIV test?

steps.text: Note the mother's status and the infant's virological and serological results.

steps.text: ASK: is the infant breastfeeding now? Was the infant breastfeeding at the time of the test or before it? Are mother and infant on ARV prophylaxis?

The mother's test is negative, or the infant's test is negative and the infant has not breastfed in the 6 weeks before the test. Routine follow-up; cotrimoxazole can be stopped.

read.text: HIV weakens a child's defences, so infections that would not usually make a child very sick can be severe. Several preventive measures keep the child's immune system as strong as possible.

Prevents PCP, other bacterial infections and malaria.

read.text: TB is a major cause of illness and death in children living with HIV, even on ART. HIV makes TB infection more likely, makes it progress faster to disease, and makes old TB come back. Start IPT only if your facility can investigate for TB.

HIV raises the risk of invasive Hib disease. An extra dose in the second year may be useful for HIV-infected children.
HIV-infected infants risk disseminated BCG disease, but infection is hard to identify at birth. Where TB and HIV are common, BCG may be given at birth to all infants.

sections.title: Feeding options for an HIV-infected mother

read.text: Explain the two national feeding strategies, and the advantages and disadvantages of breastfeeding and formula.

read.text: Infant feeding counselling is critical to prevent mother-to-child transmission. HIV-negative women and women who do not know their status (encourage them to test) should breastfeed exclusively for 6 months, then add complementary foods and continue breastfeeding to 2 years or beyond.

cards.back: Breast milk and nothing more until 6 months.
Breast milk and other foods or fluids. It increases the risk of HIV transmission, diarrhoea and other infections.

read.text: WHO asks national health authorities to choose ONE strategy for HIV-infected mothers, to give infants the greatest chance of HIV-free survival: (1) breastfeed and receive ARV interventions, OR (2) avoid all breastfeeding. The choice depends on the social and cultural context, the health services, HIV prevalence, and the main causes of child undernutrition and death.
Is this an advantage of exclusive breastfeeding or of commercial formula?

items.text: Protects the baby from many serious diseases
Carries no risk of passing HIV to the baby
Is free, always available, and needs no preparation
Others can help feed the baby
Lowers the risk of HIV compared with mixed feeding
Protects the mother from getting pregnant again too soon

read.text: What are the disadvantages of formula?
read.answer: No antibodies, so the baby is more likely to get diarrhoea, chest infections and malnutrition. It needs a steady supply of fuel and clean, boiled water; takes time to prepare fresh each time; is expensive; makes people wonder why the mother is not breastfeeding; and the mother may get pregnant again too soon.

read.text: What are the disadvantages of exclusive breastfeeding for an HIV-infected mother?
read.answer: The baby is exposed to HIV as long as she breastfeeds. People may pressure her to give water or food (mixed feeding). She needs support, and it may be hard if she works away from home.

read.text: Where policy is to breastfeed with ARVs, a mother who cannot or will not breastfeed is referred to a feeding counsellor.
Give the feeding recommendations by age, when national policy is breastfeeding with ARVs and when it is formula only.

read.text: At follow-up of a mother who breastfeeds, what do you check?
read.answer: That she breastfeeds exclusively with no other milk, water or food; often and as long as the baby wants; any feeding problem (not enough milk, crying, sore nipples); a breastfeed and her breasts if needed; that she is on ART or ARV prophylaxis and adheres; and her health, with a CD4 count in the last 6 months.

read.text: Infections like TB and diarrhoea cause loss of appetite, weight loss and acute malnutrition in HIV-infected children. Always advise the mother to continue feeding and giving fluids during illness, and to feed more after it.

cards.back: Treat it. Breastfeed at least 8 times in 24 hours; give small meals at least 5 times a day, with added oil or nuts.
Treat it, feed as above, deworm and give vitamin A if not given in the last 6 months.
Treat the thrush. Give mashed or pureed food, no spicy food; paracetamol half an hour before feeds may help in extreme cases.
Give small frequent sips and food the child likes, let the child eat before the medicine; for ritonavir, coat the tongue with peanut butter first.
Soft, varied favourite foods that do not burn the mouth (egg, mashed potato, pumpkin, avocado), small frequent feeds when the child is alert, and active feeding on the mother's lap.

read.title: Stopping breastfeeding: gradually, over one month

steps.title: Plan ahead
steps.text: Discuss why she wants to stop, and what food and milk she will give instead. Crying does not mean she has too little milk.

steps.title: Prepare the baby
steps.text: Teach the baby to drink expressed breast milk from a cup (boiled if mother and baby are not on ARVs). Replace one breastfeed with one cup feed, then more every few days. A clean finger can replace the breast for sucking.

steps.title: Stop completely
steps.text: Stop as soon as the baby is used to frequent cup feeds. Do not start again: it raises the risk of HIV. Express a little milk and use cold compresses when the breasts feel full.

steps.title: Continue ARV prophylaxis
steps.text: Continue it for one week after the baby has had no breast milk at all, and make sure she has enough.

steps.title: Family planning and CD4
steps.text: Start family planning before breastfeeding ends. Check she has had a CD4 count in the past 6 months.

cards.back: Help her make a safe and complete change to replacement feeds; arrange formula (under 6 months) or plain milk if she has no resources. Refer her for ART and give cotrimoxazole.
A suitable breast milk substitute, breast milk from a confirmed HIV-negative woman, or pasteurized milk from a breast milk bank.
Safe family foods and milk or another animal-source food every day.

options: Until one week after the last breast milk

read.text: During a sick child visit, listen for the mother's own problems, and write them at the bottom of the recording form so you remember to help her after the child. Do not make her queue twice or go elsewhere for simple problems.

cards.back: Care for her, or refer her for ART.
Engorgement, sore nipples or infection: give care or refer.
Eat well to keep up her own strength and health.
Check her immunization and give TT if needed.
Discuss methods, offer barrier contraception as well, and give at least 3 months' supply.
Screen and treat by the national STI protocol; counsel on safe sex.
Regular CD4 testing (every 6 months), sexual health services and counselling.
Partner, family, housing, childcare, workload: give ongoing counselling, refer if needed.

read.text: If she is HIV-infected, reassure her that with regular follow-up much can be done to keep her and her child well; stress good hygiene and early treatment of illness.

stages.question: What feeding advice do you give Lungile?

stages.text: Lungile has just found out she has HIV. She lives alone in a tin shack in the city, fetching water from a tap 200 metres away. Her partner works in another city. Neither he nor her mother knows her status; she is scared to tell her partner.
stages.question: What do you discuss today?

Everything about HIV in one session
Nothing: it is not your role

read.text: HIV is a retrovirus, so the drugs against it are antiretroviral drugs (ARVs). They interfere with the life cycle of the virus so it cannot make copies of itself. Giving ARVs correctly, with adherence support, is antiretroviral therapy (ART).
ART does NOT cure HIV. By stopping the virus from multiplying, it prevents damage to the immune system and improves quality of life and life expectancy.
read.label: Key point

read.text: Children's bodies handle ARVs differently, so doses are adjusted to weight as the child grows.

cards.front: It takes a lot of force
cards.back: HIV makes new copies very fast. One drug slows it; three together have a very powerful effect.
ARVs from different groups attack the virus at different steps of making copies.
HIV can change so a drug works less well. With three drugs together, it takes much longer for resistance to develop.

First-line regimens usually include 2 NsRTIs and 1 NNRTI or a boosted PI. Stavudine was used as a first-line drug and many children still take it, but it is no longer preferred.

read.text: A child with a general danger sign or a severe classification needs URGENT REFERRAL. ART is not urgent: start it once the child is stable (acute illnesses and opportunistic infections treated) and the five steps are completed.

read.title: The five steps of starting ART

steps.title: Step 1: confirm HIV infection
steps.text: Under 18 months: a positive virological (PCR) test, and the child has not breastfed for at least 6 weeks. 18 months or older: two different positive serological tests. If results disagree, refer.

steps.title: Step 2: the caregiver is able to give ART
steps.text: She is willing and able, and ideally has disclosed to another adult who can help, or is in a support group. If not: classify CONFIRMED HIV INFECTION not on ART, follow up and support her until she is ready.

steps.title: Step 3: can ART start at your facility?
steps.text: If the child weighs less than 3 kg or has TB, refer non-urgently for ART. Otherwise go to step 4.

steps.title: Step 4: record baseline information
steps.text: Weight, height and nutrition, pallor, feeding, clinical stage, and laboratory results. Do not wait for results.

steps.title: Step 5: start ART and cotrimoxazole
steps.text: With routine treatments, and follow up after one week.

read.text: All children under 5 years with CONFIRMED HIV INFECTION are eligible for ART. From 5 years, WHO 2014 used a CD4 count below 500 (priority below 350) or clinical stage 3 or 4.
read.label: Key point

read.text: WHO now recommends ART for every child living with HIV, at any age and any CD4 count.
read.label: Changed since 2014

read.title: Who starts ART at a first-level facility?

cards.back: A stable child: not ill, and no signs of advanced HIV infection.
A child under 3 kg (doses are hard), or a child with TB or suspected TB (needs investigations and dose changes). Non-urgent means soon, but not necessarily the same day.

sections.title: Prepare the caregiver for adherence: the 5 As

read.text: Use the 5 As to prepare a caregiver to give ART every day.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Adherence is the cornerstone of ART: at least 95% of doses must be taken.
read.label: Key point

read.text: Why is adherence harder for children?
read.answer: Children depend on their caregivers; parents may not want to disclose the status; there are few easy child formulations, so mixtures of pills and syrups are needed; and many medicines taste bad.

read.text: These social criteria are not a barrier to ART, but part of preparing for it: at least one caregiver who can supervise the medicine, and, if possible, disclosure to another adult in the same house who can help.

steps.title: 1. ASSESS
steps.text: Find a treatment supporter. Check the caregiver understands that ART is lifelong and has side effects.

steps.title: 2. ADVISE
steps.text: Be open, non-judgmental and patient: "I have some information about HIV and ART. Would you like to hear it?" Explain how the illness progresses and that the child's life depends on the correct dose twice a day at the right time. Do not give too much at once: spread the advice over several visits.

steps.title: 3. AGREE
steps.text: Check she is willing and motivated: "After hearing all this, how do you think your child will be able to take this treatment?" Has she kept appointments and given other medicines? Does she take her own treatment?

steps.title: 4. ASSIST
steps.text: "What problems might arise?" Help with transport and time off work, giving medicine without stigma, family support, disclosure and an adherence support group.

steps.title: 5. ARRANGE
steps.text: Arrange another session to reinforce key messages, and a support group if she wishes.

read.text: Preparing a caregiver usually takes 2 to 3 visits, the clinical team and a treatment supporter.

On abacavir, assess carefully and call for advice. Severe, generalized or peeling rash, rash on the mucosa, or rash with fever or vomiting: stop the drugs and REFER URGENTLY.
Give the drug with food. If it lasts more than 2 weeks or worsens, call for advice or refer.
Repeat the dose if the medicine is seen in the vomit or vomiting was within 30 minutes. Vomiting everything, or with severe abdominal pain or difficult breathing: REFER URGENTLY.
Use the diarrhoea charts. If due to ARVs it improves in a few weeks; if not after 2 weeks, call for advice or refer.
Paracetamol for headache. Give efavirenz at night on an empty stomach or with low-fat food. If it lasts more than 2 weeks, call for advice or refer.
If new or worse on treatment, call for advice or refer.
Consider switching from stavudine to abacavir; refer if needed.

stages.text: Each month Peter gets routine care (vitamin A, immunizations, growth monitoring, feeding counselling), continues cotrimoxazole, has new problems treated, and you ask about Lungile's health.
Lungile stops breastfeeding when Peter is 9 months old, because she now works away from home. They return 7 weeks after his last breastfeed.
stages.question: Which test now confirms Peter's status?
stages.explanation: Peter is under 18 months and has not breastfed for more than 6 weeks: a virological test confirms his status.

stages.text: You counsel Lungile, discuss disclosure and send a PCR test. Two and a half weeks later the result is positive. Lungile feels guilty that she made Peter sick; you counsel her that treatment can keep him healthy.
stages.question: How do you classify Peter now?
stages.explanation: A positive virological test, more than 6 weeks after the last breastfeed: CONFIRMED HIV INFECTION. All children under 5 with confirmed infection should receive ART.

stages.text: Peter is stable: he needs no treatment today for an acute illness or opportunistic infection. Step 1: his infection is confirmed.

Step 2: you use the 5 As with Lungile: her social situation and understanding of HIV, key information about ART and adherence, whether she can give the medicine every day and come to appointments, her support, and another session.
Step 3: Peter has no TB and weighs more than 3 kg.
stages.question: Where does Peter start ART?

stages.text: Step 4: Peter is not low weight and not anaemic. He has had pneumonia, persistent diarrhoea and ear infections in the past months, and herpes zoster is starting. You send CD4 and viral load tests.
Step 5: Peter is under 3 years and weighs 7.2 kg.
stages.question: Which regimen and doses?
options: ABC 4 ml + 3TC 4 ml + LPV/r 1.5 ml, each twice a day
ABC 6 ml + 3TC 6 ml + LPV/r 2 ml, each twice a day
stages.explanation: Under 3 years: ABC + 3TC + LPV/r. The 6 to 9.9 kg band is 4 ml, 4 ml and 1.5 ml twice a day. He also continues cotrimoxazole. You tell Lungile about side effects, and see him after one week.

sections.title: Follow-up of exposed infants and good chronic care

read.text: Make sure exposed infants are tested and followed up, and use the principles of good chronic care.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.text: Every child born to an HIV-infected mother needs follow-up for safe feeding, growth and development, HIV testing and other care. Offer a PCR test at 4 to 6 weeks (for example at the immunization visit), start cotrimoxazole, and ask the caregiver to return for the result. Reclassify the child when the result is known, and give care for the new classification.
How can a clinic find more HIV-exposed infants?
read.answer: Have a system in every clinic to identify infants and offer testing. Integrated maternal and child health clinics see mothers and children together; a family-based model links the records of the whole family, so when a parent comes you ask about the children and partner.

read.text: HIV is a chronic disease. Good chronic care recognizes that the mother must learn to manage her child's condition, often while coping with her own illness: a double burden.

1. Develop a treatment partnership with the mother and child
  2. Focus on their concerns and priorities
  3. Use IMCI counselling skills and the 5 As
  4. Support self-management
  5. Organize proactive follow-up
  6. Involve expert patients, peer educators and support staff
  7. Link the family to community resources and support
  8. Use written information to document, monitor and remind
  9. Work as a multidisciplinary clinical team
  10. Assure continuity of care

cards.back: An agreement to work together towards an agreed goal: both share responsibility and treat each other with respect; one partner does not have all the power.
Find out the real reason she came: illness, fear, or a psychosocial need, and address it.
Leave the mother as much in charge as possible: she takes responsibility for daily treatment, and feels more in control.
A nurse, clinical officer, an ART aid for education and adherence, and a doctor.

sections.title: Follow-up of a child on ART: the four steps

read.text: Follow up a child on ART in four steps, and know when to refer urgently or non-urgently.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.title: Follow-up of a child on ART
read.caption: Watch this first.

read.title: The four steps of each follow-up visit

steps.title: 1. Assess and classify
steps.text: Ask about problems and care elsewhere since the last visit. Check general danger signs, ART severe signs and the main symptoms.

steps.title: 2. Monitor progress on ART and cotrimoxazole
steps.text: Growth and nutrition, development, adherence, side effects, clinical stage and laboratory results.

steps.title: 3. Continue ART and other medicines
steps.text: If stable, continue the same first-line regimen, adjusting doses to weight.

steps.title: 4. Counsel
steps.text: Progress, feeding, adherence, side effects, disclosure, support for the caregiver; check the family gets care. If well, follow up in one month.

read.text: ART severe signs: severe skin rash; difficulty breathing with severe abdominal pain; yellow eyes; or two of fever, vomiting and rash in a child on abacavir. Give pre-referral treatment and REFER URGENTLY.
read.label: Key point

read.text: How often does the child miss doses?

items.text: No dose missed this month
One dose missed last week
Two doses missed each week
Three or more doses missed each week

read.explanation: Poor adherence means missing more than two doses a week. Ask kindly when the last dose was missed; a pill count can help. Praise good adherence at every visit.

read.text:
Viral load (copies/ml)Meaning and action
Below 400ART is working well. Routine follow-up; repeat after a year.
400 to 1000Improvement needed. Step up adherence counselling; repeat after 6 months.
Above 1000ARVs not working well (poor adherence or resistance). Step up counselling, repeat after 3 months; if still above 1000, refer.

CD4 count and percentage are repeated after 6 months, after 1 year, then every year. Normal CD4 counts are higher in young children, so they cannot be read like an adult's. Lack of laboratory tests should never stop a child from receiving ART.

cards.back: Not gaining weight for 3 months, or losing milestones.
Poor adherence despite counselling.
Significant side effects despite good management.
A higher clinical stage than before, CD4 much lower than before, or viral load above 400 despite counselling (on LPV/r: LDL above 3.5 or triglycerides above 5.6 mmol/L).

read.text: A new or recurrent stage 3 or 4 event after at least 24 weeks of ART, in a child who takes the medicine well, may mean treatment failure. Only experienced clinicians change to second-line treatment.
Replace stavudine when fat changes appear, support disclosure to the child, and follow up children on ART.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.text: Nurses at primary level prescribe only first-line regimens and do not change ARVs without an expert, with one exception: stavudine. It causes peripheral neuropathy (tingling in the hands and feet) and lipodystrophy: the arms, legs, buttocks and cheeks become THIN while the breasts, tummy and back of the neck become FAT. This may not go away, so switch early to abacavir. A child doing well on stavudine stays on it.
Disclosure to the child

Disclosing the HIV status to the child is the caregiver's role, with support from the health worker. It is a process, not an event: partial disclosure first (without naming HIV, for example the "soldier story"), then full disclosure over time, fitted to the child's understanding, development, health and situation. There is no fixed age; questions about the clinic or the medicine, or refusing treatment, are signs the child wants to know more. Adolescents should know their status.

cards.back: Better adjustment, self-esteem and adherence, fewer risky behaviours, and stronger family ties.
Less part in treatment, more psychological problems, isolation, hurtful fantasies about the illness, and accidental disclosure that breaks the child's trust in adults.

stages.text: There are no new problems and no care elsewhere. Peter has no general danger sign, no main symptom, and no severe skin rash, difficult breathing, yellow eyes, fever or vomiting. You screen for TB.

He has gained a little weight, to 7.4 kg. Lungile has given every dose and brought the containers. There is no change in side effects or stage. His CD4 count is 600 cells/mm3, and the viral load is detectable but not high.
stages.question: What do you do?
options: Continue the same ART and cotrimoxazole, praise her, counsel and arrange the next visit
stages.explanation: Peter is stable. Counsel on his progress, adherence (his viral load is still detectable), side effects, disclosure and support.

Stage a child with confirmed HIV infection using the WHO paediatric clinical staging.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.text: Clinical staging estimates how damaged a child's immune system is, from the child's signs and symptoms (and laboratory tests if possible). Use it only for children with confirmed HIV infection. Choose the highest stage that applies. Stages 1 and 2: the immune system is not yet seriously affected and most conditions are managed at first level. Stages 3 and 4: advanced immune deficiency; most conditions need urgent referral.

read.title: The four stages (WHO 2005 revised paediatric staging)

cards.back: No symptoms, or only persistent generalized lymphadenopathy.

Enlarged liver or spleen, enlarged parotid, skin conditions (prurigo, seborrhoeic dermatitis, extensive molluscum or warts, fungal nail infection, herpes zoster), recurrent mouth ulcers, angular cheilitis, gum erythema, recurrent or chronic respiratory infections (sinusitis, ear infections, otorrhoea).

Moderate unexplained malnutrition not responding to treatment; oral thrush (after the newborn period); oral hairy leukoplakia; unexplained diarrhoea over 14 days or fever over 1 month not responding to treatment; recurrent severe bacterial pneumonia; pulmonary or lymph node TB; symptomatic LIP; necrotizing gingivitis; chronic HIV lung disease; anaemia, neutropenia or low platelets for over a month.

Severe unexplained wasting, stunting or malnutrition not responding to treatment; PCP; oesophageal thrush; herpes simplex ulcers for over a month; 2 or more severe bacterial infections a year (not pneumonia); Kaposi's sarcoma; extrapulmonary TB; toxoplasma brain abscess; cryptococcal meningitis; HIV encephalopathy; rectal fistula.

read.text: Children are staged even when they are on ART, because a change of stage shows how they respond. A child with suspected severe HIV disease whose infection cannot be confirmed needs referral.

Herpes zoster
Recurrent ear discharge
Oral thrush in a 2-year-old
Pulmonary TB
