read.text:
Look back at the main points:

  • A positive serological test cannot confirm HIV under 18 months; a positive virological test confirms it at any age.
  • A negative test only rules out infection once the child has not breastfed for at least 6 weeks.
  • Three classifications: CONFIRMED HIV INFECTION, HIV EXPOSED, HIV INFECTION UNLIKELY.
  • Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis for exposed and infected children; ARV prophylaxis for exposed infants; IPT, immunization and vitamin A.
  • All children under 5 with confirmed infection start ART after the five steps; adherence of at least 95% is essential.
  • Each follow-up visit of a child on ART has four steps; ART severe signs need urgent referral.
Answer the same questions as before the module.
Then take the logbook test. You may use your chart booklet, but not the module.

modules.title: Module 9: Care of the well child

read.text: See what well child care covers, and take the pre-test.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: A well child is a child who comes to the health facility for preventive services: immunizations, feeding advice, and growth and development monitoring. You use the same IMNCI skills as for the sick child: ask questions, listen, praise good practices, advise in simple language, and check understanding. Even when the clinic is busy, take time to assess a well child properly.

More than 200 million children under 5 are not developing to their full potential because they did not get simple, essential care. Risks include stunting, iron and iodine deficiency, frequent illness, and too little help to learn, explore and communicate.
What you will practise

• Feeding infants and young children well
  • Care for healthy growth and development
  • Immunization, vitamin A and deworming
  • Water, sanitation and hygiene
  • Prevention of childhood accidents
Which part of the recording form is used in this module?

read.caption: The national recording form: immunization and feeding

read.text: Before you begin

sections.title: Growth and development: what they are

read.text: Tell growth from development, and name the four kinds of skills a child develops.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Care of the well child
read.caption: Watch this first.

cards.back: An increase in physical size, composition and distribution of tissues: weight, length and height.

The gradual unfolding of what a child can do: talk, walk, run, solve problems, receive affection and express emotions. It needs good health and nutrition, chances to explore, and a safe, nurturing home.
Physical skills such as reaching and grabbing: planned eye and hand movement, muscle control and strength.
Exploring and learning through seeing, hearing, moving and touching; recognizing people, things and sounds; comparing sizes and shapes.
Communicating interests and needs, with words and without.
Receiving and expressing emotions and affection appropriately.

read.text: Which skill is the child using?

items.text: Sees a ball rolling and tries to take and hold it
Cries and reaches for the ball when it rolls away
Examines the ball's shape and size
Smiles at his mother when she talks to him about the ball

read.text: Health workers need to understand growth and development to monitor progress, find delays early, counsel caregivers and treat. Poor growth and development can also reflect poverty, little education, and poor access to food, safe water and health services.

sections.title: Growth monitoring: why, what and how often

read.text: Explain growth monitoring and promotion, name the three growth indicators, and know how often to measure.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Growth monitoring and promotion (GMP) detects poor growth early, so it can be corrected. It is not only measuring: you use the results to counsel the caregiver on what she can do at home.

GMP helps you to:

  • Analyse the causes of poor growth: acute or chronic illness, acute malnutrition, feeding problems
  • Show the caregiver the child's growth on the growth chart
  • Agree with the caregiver on actions at home, early
  • Link families to community and nutrition services
  • Keep the child in regular contact with the clinic

cards.back: Low = UNDERWEIGHT. Changes quickly with health, so it is the measure used to monitor growth in infants and young children.
Low = STUNTING (chronic malnutrition): the result of long-term poor nutrition.
Low = WASTING (acute malnutrition), as in Module 6.

read.text:
AgeHow often
Birth to 2 yearsMonthly: weight every month, length every 3 months
2 to 5 yearsEvery 3 months: weight and height at every visit

cards.back: Length (lying) under 2 years; height (standing) from 2 years. Under 2 measured standing: add 0.7 cm. 2 years or older measured lying: subtract 0.7 cm.
A solar, taring scale (it can subtract the mother's weight). A Salter scale can be used until one is available.
A wooden length board in two or three pieces, joined for a tall child.
Growth charts for each visit, and the schedules for vaccines, vitamin A and deworming. Separate books for boys and girls.

read.text: Use every growth monitoring visit, in the clinic or at outreach, to give other services: assessment, treatment, vaccination, vitamin A, deworming and psychosocial support.
Use the child health book with the caregiver, and decide whether a child's growth and development are normal.
read.label: In this lesson

steps.title: Why
steps.text: Explain why growth matters, even if the child looks healthy next to the other children at home.

steps.title: The book
steps.text: Explain the child health book. Every child should get one soon after birth; bring it to every visit.

steps.title: The chart
steps.text: Use the growth chart to show how the child is growing, and the pattern over time.

steps.title: What else is due
steps.text: Show the feeding advice and the schedules in the book, and remind her of the services due today.

read.text: The mother's health is important for the child's health. Ask about her pregnancy, delivery and health since.
read.label: Remember

stages.text: Samson comes for growth monitoring and vitamin A. He weighs 8 kg and is 64 cm long. On the boys' chart, 8 kg at 64 cm is above the median line.
stages.question: What do you tell his mother?
options: He is growing well; praise her and continue

stages.text: Jandika comes for growth monitoring. He weighs 8 kg and is 71 cm long. His weight-for-length is between 0 and -1: not wasted. But on the length-for-age chart he is below -3.
stages.question: What does this show, and what do you do?
options: Severe stunting: refer (not urgently) to find and treat the cause
stages.explanation: Advise his mother not to delay the hospital visit.

read.text: Explain bonding and attachment to a caregiver, and tell sensitivity from responsiveness.
read.label: In this lesson

cards.back: The mother forms a relationship with her new baby, starting in the first hours after birth. Harmed by long separation after birth, poor health or depression of the mother (often undetected), abuse or neglect, or a low birth weight or sick baby.
The baby forms a relationship with the mother or main caregiver during the first two years, especially at 2 to 7 months, and develops a personal way of communicating with her.

read.text:
Poor attachment can lead to:

  • Difficulty trusting others; depression or rage
  • Failure to thrive, physically and emotionally
  • Difficulty adapting to change
  • Later, behaviour problems, poor relations with peers, poor problem solving and low self-esteem

cards.back: Being aware of the baby's signals and reading them correctly; accepting the child's interests; seeing the child as a separate person, from his point of view.
Responding to the signal quickly and appropriately, for example seeing that the baby is hungry and feeding him. A caregiver must be sensitive to be responsive.

read.text: Sara and her son John: sensitivity or responsiveness?

items.text: Sara hears John crying
Sara picks John up to soothe his crying
While bathing John, Sara notices a rash on his leg
Sara sees John watching the branches blowing in the wind
Sara says: "Do you see the wind blowing? The leaves are blowing!"
Sara notices John is feeding less than usual
Sara offers John a food he likes to see if he will eat

read.text: Sara's grandmother says John should be left alone so he grows strong and independent. What do you tell Sara?
read.answer: Explain the benefits of bonding and attachment for John's growth and for his skills, with clear examples Sara can share with her grandmother: a child who is answered when he signals grows more secure, curious and able to learn.

read.text: Recommend play and communication activities for the child's age, and show how to make toys at home.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Play and communication activities stimulate learning, improve care (including feeding), strengthen the caregiver's skills, and improve the interaction between caregiver and child.

read.title: Care for child development
read.caption: WHO Care for Child Development CD: case stories on child development.

cards.back: Play: let the baby see, hear, feel, move arms and legs freely and touch you; skin-to-skin; gently soothe and stroke. Communicate: look into the baby's eyes and talk, also during breastfeeding.
Play: move colourful things for the baby to see and reach; a shaker rattle, a ring on a string. Communicate: smile and laugh, talk, copy the baby's sounds and gestures.
Play: clean, safe household things to handle, bang and drop: containers with lids, a metal pot and spoon. Communicate: respond to sounds and interests; call the child's name and see the response.
Play: hide a toy and let the child find it; peek-a-boo; a doll with a face. Communicate: name things and people; teach gestures like waving bye-bye.
Play: things to stack and to put in and out of containers. Communicate: ask simple questions; respond to attempts to talk; show and talk about nature, pictures and people.
Play: pictures, face puzzles, shapes to sort by colour, a soft ball, chalk and a flat stone, a home-made book. Communicate: encourage the child to talk and tell stories; answer questions.

read.text: Toys do not need to be bought. Make some at the clinic from jars, stones, cloth, cardboard and old magazines, and show caregivers how easy they are to make and use.

read.title: Using the chart with a caregiver

steps.title: Find the age
steps.text: Find the child's age group and its activities, and explain the chart.

steps.title: Teach
steps.text: Explain how to play and communicate, demonstrate, then watch her practise and give feedback.

steps.title: At home
steps.text: Explain how to use the activities regularly at home, and ask checking questions.

read.text: Which is a good checking question?
options: What activities can you do to play with your child?
Did the nurse explain how to play with your child?
read.explanation: It cannot be answered yes or no.

read.text: Beta says her son Rakim, 4 months, is too little to understand play or talk. What do you say?
read.answer: Development begins at birth: even in his first hours a baby connects with people and his surroundings. Show Beta how Rakim already communicates and plays now: following her voice, reaching, smiling.

read.title: How to check some milestones in the clinic

cards.back: Lay the child face up and gently pull to sitting by both hands; make a sound with keys; ask the mother to make a joyful sound. The child holds the head up, turns it, responds to voice and smiles.
Sit the child on a safe flat surface with a toy to hold. The child sits without using the hands for at least 10 seconds, and brings objects to the mouth.

Short phrases, kicks a ball on request, jumps with both feet, turns pages one at a time, points to named pictures.

stages.text: Manka was born at term 5 months ago. She got neck control at 5 months and cannot yet sit without support. Her mother is worried.
stages.question: What do you advise?
options: This can be normal: children sit without support at 5 to 7 months; keep coming for monitoring

stages.text: Ikupa is 36 months old. She walks only with support, says about 10 words and drinks from a cup.
stages.question: What do you advise?
options: Her milestones are those of 8 to 11 months: refer (not urgently) for assessment within a few days
stages.explanation: At 3 years she should run, jump, stand on one foot and use plurals.

read.text: Build the mother's confidence, then counsel on common feeding problems and follow them up.
read.label: In this lesson

steps.title: Build confidence first
steps.text: Praise good feeding practices; encourage her to feed the same way in illness and health. Avoid judgemental words.

steps.title: Counsel for the age
steps.text: If the child is entering a new age group, explain the new recommendations (for example, at almost 6 months, good complementary foods and when to start).

steps.title: Explain what is not followed
steps.text: Explain the recommendations that are not being followed, and make suggestions.

cards.back: Check and improve positioning and attachment (Module 2). A breast problem may need a trained breastfeeding counsellor.

cards.front: Under 6 months, other milk or foods
cards.back: Aim to return to more or exclusive breastfeeding: more frequent, longer breastfeeds day and night, and gradually reduce other milk or food. If breastfeeding is not possible, teach correct preparation of breast-milk substitutes, used within one hour.
Recommend a cup: it is easier to keep clean and does not interfere with breastfeeding.
Sit with the child and encourage him to eat. He needs his own serving, not a shared plate with siblings.
Offer the foods recommended for his age, as often as recommended; breastfeed more often and longer; small, frequent, soft, liked foods. Discourage snacks and juices that only fill him up.

read.text:
Encourage a young child to eat

  • Offer small amounts when the child is alert and happy, and more if he shows interest
  • Food of suitable consistency, not too thick or dry
  • A suitable spoon, food within reach, the child on the caregiver's lap
  • Encourage with words, smiles and songs. A child who gets more attention for refusing food may eat less.

Sudan national booklet: Follow up a FEEDING PROBLEM in 7 days: reassess feeding, ask how she has carried out the advice, and counsel on any new or continuing problem. WHO module (page 39): Follow-up in 5 days; if the child is very low weight for age, also return 30 days after the first visit to check weight gain.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

stages.text: At the first visit, a 3-month-old was getting 2 or 3 bottles of milk a day and some breastfeeds. The health worker advised more frequent, longer breastfeeds and less other milk. Now the mother gives 1 bottle a day and breastfeeds 6 or more times in 24 hours.
stages.question: What do you do?
options: Praise her, then suggest stopping the other milk and breastfeeding 8 or more times in 24 hours, and see her again

read.text: Give the feeding recommendations for the child's age, in sickness and in health.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: First ask how the child is fed now; then give only the advice needed for the child's age and situation. The recommendations are the same when the child is sick and when well. During illness offer the recommended foods as often as recommended; after illness, good feeding makes up the weight lost.
Use the national mother card for your counselling. The age groups below are those of the WHO module.

cards.back: Breastfeed exclusively, as often as the child wants, day and night, at least 8 times in 24 hours. No other food or fluid, not even water (medicines and vitamins only if needed).

Breastfeed as often as the child wants, breast milk first. Start 2–3 teaspoons of soft porridge or mashed food and build up: 3 meals plus healthy snacks a day if breastfed, 5 meals if not. Not breastfed: formula, or 3 cups of full-cream cow's milk from 9 months.

Breastfeed as often as the child wants. Complementary or chopped and mashed family foods 5 times a day, with protein at least once a day and fruit or vegetables twice. Not breastfed: full-cream milk every day. Active feeding.
Family foods, 3 meals a day plus 2 nutritious snacks between meals (bread with peanut butter, fruit, full-cream milk). Continue active feeding; offer a refused food several times.

read.text:
Include all food groups

  • Cereals, roots and tubers: rice, wheat, maize, millet, sorghum, cassava, potatoes
  • Animal foods and legumes: meat, chicken, fish, eggs, milk, cheese, yoghurt, chickpeas, lentils, beans
  • Green leafy and orange vegetables; fruits, mashed
  • Oils and fats, preferably seed oils such as groundnut or sunflower

Vitamin CMany fruits and vegetables, potatoes

cards.back: Clean hands, utensils, water and food; boil drinking water and milk; keep food well cooked and covered.
Ready-made jars of baby food (costly, unreliable, often lacking nutrients), fruit juice, tea and sugary drinks.
Feed slowly and patiently, without forcing; own serving; eye contact and talk. An adequate serving means the child wants no more after active feeding.

read.text: About 9 out of 10 cases of diarrhoea come from unsafe water or poor sanitation and hygiene, which also lead to pneumonia and worms that cause anaemia. The key interventions are cheap: safe drinking water, hand washing, and toilets in the home and community.

cards.back: Before preparing food, before eating, before feeding a child.
After using the toilet, and after cleaning a child who has used it.
After coughing, sneezing or blowing the nose; before and after cleaning a child's face; after handling animals, animal waste or rubbish.

read.text:
How

read.text: Babies explore by putting things in the mouth. Ask where the child rests and plays. Keep the area clean and free of small objects, sharp things like glass or stones, and heat such as fires, heaters, lamps and electric sockets; a mat that is shaken clean helps.

sections.title: Immunization: the schedule and checking status

read.text: Use the national schedule to decide which vaccines a child needs today.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Immunization is the most cost-effective way to reduce illness and death in children. Every child should complete the schedule before the first birthday. Check every child's status at every visit, and give missed vaccines that day. Too early, protection may not be adequate; late, the child is at risk.

AgeVaccines (Sudan national schedule)
BirthOPV 0, BCG
6 weeksOPV 1, Pentavalent 1, PCV 1, Rota 1, IPV 1
10 weeksOPV 2, Pentavalent 2, PCV 2, Rota 2
14 weeksOPV 3, Pentavalent 3, PCV 3, Rota 3, IPV 2
9 monthsMR, Men A, Yellow fever
18 monthsMR (booster)

Sudan national booklet: The national schedule adds IPV at 6 and 14 weeks, gives MR (measles-rubella), meningitis A and yellow fever at 9 months, and an MR booster at 18 months. Keep 4 weeks between doses of pentavalent, PCV, OPV and Rota, and 8 weeks between the IPV doses. WHO module (page 54): Birth BCG and OPV 0; 6, 10 and 14 weeks DPT-HepB-Hib (pentavalent), pneumococcal, rota and OPV; measles at 9 months. Repeated doses at least 4 weeks apart.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

cards.back: Not after 14 days of age: give OPV 1 at 6 weeks instead, with the other 6-week vaccines.
Not after 1 year of age.
At any age if not given before; over 1 year, only after a negative Mantoux test.
Give the OPV dose that is due, but do not count it; ask the mother to return in 4 weeks for an extra dose.

steps.title: Ask for the child health book
steps.text: Compare the dates with the schedule, and find the vaccines missed or due today.

steps.title: No book?
steps.text: Ask what the child has received. If you doubt the report, vaccinate. Give her a child health book to bring each time.

steps.title: Give and record
steps.text: Unless the child is being referred, give the vaccines today, record the dates, and write the return date.

read.text: Counsel on common reactions to vaccines, and vaccinate sick children unless there is a true contraindication.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: An adverse event following immunization (AEFI) is an unwanted event after a vaccine; it may be caused by the vaccine or happen by chance. Most are minor: low fever, pain, redness or swelling at the injection site, crying and irritability. Explain them at vaccination, so they do not keep the mother, or other mothers, away next time. Extensive swelling of the whole limb is not common: the child returns to the facility.
For fever over 38.5 °C after vaccination give paracetamol (15 mg/kg a dose), for up to 2 days. Do not give paracetamol at the time of vaccination.

cards.back: Common illness, including malnutrition. If a sick child is well enough to go home, vaccinate.
Do not give BCG to a child with HIV infection (AIDS).
Do not give it to a child who had convulsions (or shock) within 72 hours of the last dose, or who has a neurological disease.
If you refer the child, you need not vaccinate first; the hospital decides, so referral is not delayed.

read.text: Vaccinate today (if due)?

read.text: Also advise the mother to have the other children in the family vaccinated.
Give routine vitamin A and deworming at the right age and interval, and record them.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Vitamin A protects the eyes and the lining of the airways, gut and urinary tract, and helps resist severe infection. Deficiency is the leading cause of preventable blindness in children and increases deaths from measles, diarrhoea and pneumonia. Good vitamin A status at 6–59 months cuts measles deaths by half and diarrhoea deaths by a third.

AgeRoutine vitamin A
6 months up to 12 months100 000 IU (blue capsule)
12 months up to 5 years200 000 IU (red capsule)

Sudan national booklet: Give the first dose any time after 6 months, then every 6 months up to 5 years. Do not give it if a dose was given in the last 6 months or the child is on RUTF. Look for doses from campaigns on the child card. WHO module (page 60): The same schedule; the WHO table also allows several smaller capsules (for example 2 × 100 000 IU or 4 × 50 000 IU for 200 000 IU).
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: Cut the nipple of the capsule with a clean blade or scissors (or pierce it with a clean, new needle) and squeeze the contents into the child's mouth. Record the date: doses less than 6 months apart risk overdose.
Deworming

Roundworm, hookworm and whipworm cause loss of micronutrients, poor appetite, anaemia, poor growth and malnutrition. From 12 months, check at every visit whether the child had a deworming dose in the last 6 months; if not, give one.

Medicine, single dose every 6 months1 up to 2 years2 up to 5 years
Albendazole 400 mg tablet½ tablet (200 mg)1 tablet (400 mg)
Mebendazole 500 mg tablet½ tablet (250 mg)1 tablet (500 mg)
Chewable tablets are best. Under 3 years, crush the tablet between two spoons and add water. In the national chart booklet, mebendazole for a child with ANAEMIA is the syrup course in Module 6.

read.text: Counsel families on preventing road injuries, drowning, burns, falls and poisoning.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Injuries are a growing problem in developing countries; nearly all are unintentional (accidents), and for every death many more children are left disabled. Ask about the home, where the child plays, how the child travels, how water is stored, and how the family cooks, heats and lights the home, then advise.

cards.back: Children do not play near the road; supervise play. Helmets on bicycles and motorcycles; seat belts or child seats in cars. Do not leave preschool children in the care of other children. Communities: pavements, safe playgrounds, speed limits.
Remove or cover toilet pits, wells and ponds; cover buckets and water drums; supervise children near any water, even a bath; flotation devices when swimming.

No playing with fire; raised, protected cooking areas with pot handles out of reach; do not hold the baby while cooking; supervise children by a fire; never leave children alone or locked in; no candle or kerosene lamp left lit while sleeping.
Guards on beds, stairs, windows and roofs; supervise children at play.

Keep medicines and poisons out of reach, in child-resistant packs and their original labelled containers. Never store kerosene or poisons in soda or water bottles. Do not send children to fetch or give medicines.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 5: Exercise C (Kareem, 5 months)
narrative: Kareem is 5 months old. He weighs 5.2 kg. His axillary temperature is 37.5 °C. His mother said he is not eating well. She said he feels hot, and she wants a health worker to help him.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 5: Exercise D (Dolma, 12 months)
narrative: Dolma is 12 months old. She weighs 7.2 kg. Her axillary temperature is 36.5 °C. Her mother brought Dolma to the health centre today because she feels hot.

Dolma has no general danger signs. She does not have cough or difficult breathing. When asked about diarrhoea, the mother said, "Yes, Dolma has had diarrhoea for 2 to 3 days." She has not seen any blood in the stool. Dolma has not been lethargic or unconscious. Her eyes are not sunken. She drinks normally. Her skin pinch returns immediately.

The health worker said, "You brought Dolma today because she feels hot. I will check her for fever." Her mother said that Dolma has felt hot for 2 days. She has not had measles within the last 3 months. There is no stiff neck and no runny nose.
Dolma has a dry, generalized rash. She also has red eyes. She has a negative malaria test.

She has no general danger sign and no stiff neck, and her malaria test is negative: FEVER: NO MALARIA.

She has a generalized rash and red eyes, so she has signs of measles. With no mouth ulcers, no pus draining from the eye and no clouding of the cornea, she is also classified MEASLES and gets vitamin A.
Her diarrhoea has no signs of dehydration: NO DEHYDRATION.

questions.question: It is best for a 3-month-old HIV-infected child to be exclusively breastfed.
A 2-week-old of unknown status, born to an HIV-negative mother, should never be breastfed.
questions.explain: The child should be exclusively breastfed: there is no risk of HIV from this mother.

questions.question: A breastfeeding child of an HIV-infected woman can continue breastfeeding up to 12 months of age.
questions.explain: Exclusively until 6 months, then with safe complementary foods.

questions.question: A 5-month-old whose mother is HIV-negative should breastfeed as often as he wants, day and night.
A 9-month-old with a positive virological test can continue breastfeeding.
All breastfeeding HIV-infected women pass HIV to their infants.
questions.explain: Without prevention, about 15% of children are infected through breastfeeding.

questions.question: A child born to a mother of unknown HIV status should be given formula.
questions.explain: All women of unknown status are counselled to breastfeed exclusively for 6 months (and encouraged to test).

questions.question: ARVs given to an HIV-infected mother or her exposed infant greatly reduce the risk of transmission through breastfeeding.
Traci is born to an HIV-positive mother. When should she begin family foods, and which foods?
points: At 6 months of age
Porridge and a mix of local foods: eggs, mashed vegetables, beans, meat or liver
Add oil, margarine or peanut paste if she is not growing well
Increase the number of meals as she grows

questions.question: Why is it important to use 3 drugs in ART for children?
points: ARVs work best in combination against HIV
Combination prevents rapid drug resistance

questions.question: A 2-month-old with a positive PCR test.
A 12-month-old with a positive PCR test.
A 2-month-old breastfeeding child with a positive serological test.
questions.explain: Send a PCR test.

questions.question: An 18-month-old breastfeeding child with two positive serological tests.
A 9-month-old breastfeeding child with a negative PCR test; the mother is HIV-infected.
questions.explain: Repeat the test 6 weeks after breastfeeding stops; the test depends on the child's age then.

questions.question: A 19-month-old with a positive serological test; the second test is negative.
questions.explain: Discordant results: send a confirmatory test as the national procedure says, or refer.

questions.question: A 9-month-old with a negative PCR test, last breastfed 3 months ago.
An 18-month-old with a negative serological test, last breastfed one week ago.
questions.explain: Repeat a serological test in 5 weeks, that is 6 weeks after breastfeeding stopped.

options: Follow the guidance for children 5 years and older

options: Follow the guidance for children 5 years and older

questions.question: 9 years old, CONFIRMED HIV INFECTION.
options: Follow the guidance for children 5 years and older
questions.explain: WHO 2014: from 5 years, CD4 below 500 or clinical stage 3 or 4. WHO now recommends ART at any age.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 8: Exercise J (ART doses)

ABC liquid + 3TC liquid + LPV/r liquid: 4 ml + 4 ml + 1.5 ml, each twice a day
ABC 2 tablets + 3TC 2 tablets twice a day, EFV 1 tablet a day
questions.explain: Under 3 years: the LPV/r regimen. (The WHO key gives efavirenz, which this module says is for 3 years and older.)

options: ABC 3 tablets + 3TC 3 tablets twice a day, EFV 1.5 tablets once a day (evening)
ABC 2 tablets + 3TC 2 tablets twice a day, EFV 1 tablet once a day
ABC liquid + 3TC liquid + LPV/r liquid: 6 ml + 6 ml + 2 ml twice a day

questions.question: A 4-month-old weighing 5 kg.
options: ABC liquid + 3TC liquid + LPV/r liquid: 3 ml + 3 ml + 1 ml, each twice a day
ABC liquid + 3TC liquid + LPV/r liquid: 4 ml + 4 ml + 1.5 ml, each twice a day
ABC 3 ml + 3TC 1 tablet + LPV/r 1 ml twice a day

questions.question: A 13-month-old weighing 12 kg.
options: ABC liquid + 3TC liquid + LPV/r liquid: 6 ml + 6 ml + 2 ml, each twice a day
ABC 2 tablets + 3TC 2 tablets twice a day, EFV 1 tablet a day
ABC liquid + 3TC liquid + LPV/r liquid: 3 ml + 3 ml + 1 ml twice a day

questions.question: A 3-year-old weighing 14.5 kg.
options: ABC 2.5 tablets + 3TC 2.5 tablets twice a day, EFV 1.5 tablets once a day
ABC 2 tablets + 3TC 2 tablets twice a day, EFV 1 tablet once a day
ABC liquid + 3TC liquid + LPV/r liquid: 6 ml + 6 ml + 2 ml twice a day

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 8: Exercise K (where to start ART)
narrative: Sister Bhengu works in a small rural clinic; a doctor visits once a week. All these children have confirmed HIV infection. Decide for each child.

questions.question: Leatile, 4 years, has CHRONIC EAR INFECTION and no other problem. His CD4 count is 200 cells/mm3.
questions.explain: (The WHO case also said he has signs of severe acute malnutrition, which conflicts with the key; that detail was removed.)

questions.question: Ofentse, 3 years, has been diagnosed with TB.
questions.explain: TB: refer non-urgently for ART.

questions.question: Luke, 2 months, was confirmed HIV-infected in hospital with severe pneumonia. He is well now and weighs 4.5 kg; his CD4 result is not back.
questions.explain: Do not wait for the CD4 result.

questions.question: Lentswe, 4 years, still breathes fast (50 a minute) after 5 days of antibiotic for PNEUMONIA. CD4 150.
questions.explain: His pneumonia is not improving.

questions.question: Owethu, 11 months, came to start ART today. She has had fever since yesterday, and is lethargic: she does not respond when spoken to or when hands are clapped.
questions.explain: Lethargy is a general danger sign.

questions.question: A 3-month-old, well, who weighs 2.8 kg.
questions.explain: Under 3 kg: refer non-urgently for ART.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 8: Exercise L (side effects)
narrative: Which drug or drugs cause each side effect? Tick all that apply.

questions.question: Severe abdominal pain with difficult breathing (could be pancreatitis)
Tingling or numbness in the feet or hands (neuropathy)
Yellow eyes (liver toxicity)
Severe skin rash
Fever, vomiting and rash together (hypersensitivity)
Changes in fat distribution
Difficulty sleeping and nightmares
Pallor (anaemia)

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 8: Exercise M (Akshay and Nancy)
narrative: Read the cases and decide.

questions.question: Akshay is 30 months old, HIV EXPOSED, with severe oral thrush. He weighs 10 kg and is 75 cm long; his weight has not changed for 3 months. He has SOME ANAEMIA (Hb 8 g/dl). Two serological tests are positive. CD4 250 cells/mm3 (12%). His mother has taken ART every day for a year, is supported by her own mother who knows her status, and asks for ART for Akshay. Is he eligible? What do you record?
points: Yes: confirmed infection (two positive serological tests) and under 5
His mother is willing and has disclosed to an adult
No TB and over 3 kg
SOME ANAEMIA: the ART initiation form says to refer; treat the anaemia and thrush
When ART starts, under 3 years: ABC 6 ml + 3TC 6 ml + LPV/r 2 ml twice a day (10 to 13.9 kg), with cotrimoxazole
Follow up after one week
questions.explain: The WHO key starts ART at the clinic with efavirenz and iron. Efavirenz is for 3 years and older, and the form refers SOME ANAEMIA, so this answer follows the module's own rules.

questions.question: Nancy is 6 months old. She was PCR positive at 6 weeks; CD4 800 cells/mm3 (30%). She is breastfeeding and well. Her mother has told no one at home, but attends the clinic support group and is committed to giving ARVs twice a day. Is Nancy eligible for ART?
options: No: her mother has not disclosed at home
questions.explain: She has confirmed infection and is under 5. Being in a support group meets the caregiver step.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 8: Exercise N (follow-up care)
narrative: Are these statements true or false?

questions.question: A child keeps the classification from the first visit, and follow-up care always follows it.
questions.explain: Children are reclassified with new test results, and care follows the new classification.

questions.question: Only children under 24 months are started on ART.
questions.explain: WHO 2014: all children under 5 with confirmed infection.

questions.question: All children of HIV-positive women should be identified and offered a PCR test at 4 to 6 weeks.
Sami, 8 months, had a negative PCR while breastfeeding. He is re-tested once breastfeeding has stopped for 4 weeks.
questions.explain: After 6 weeks.

questions.question: Cotrimoxazole is an important part of follow-up care for HIV-exposed and infected children.
Jyothi is classified HIV EXPOSED. You follow her up and test for HIV as soon as possible.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 8: Exercise O (follow-up on ART)
narrative: These children are on ART. What will you do?

questions.question: Mandla, 4 years, has been on stavudine, lamivudine and lopinavir/ritonavir for 3 years. His face and arms look thin and his body fatter.
options: Check his viral load: below 400, replace stavudine with abacavir; above 400, refer non-urgently
Stop all ARVs and refer urgently
Reassure the mother; nothing needs to change

questions.question: Ross, 9 months, started ART 2 weeks ago. He does not want to eat and has diarrhoea, with sunken eyes but no other sign of dehydration.
options: Explain it may be the ARVs and should improve in weeks, stress adherence, treat the diarrhoea and follow up
questions.explain: Treat the diarrhoea by the chart (continue feeding, extra fluid) and see him again if it does not improve.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 8: Exercise P (follow-up visits)
narrative: Decide what to do at these follow-up visits.

questions.question: Nancy, now 12 months, has done well on ART. Since yesterday she vomits after every meal, and her mother sees that her eyes are yellow.
options: Stop the ARVs and refer urgently
Continue ART and follow up in a month
questions.explain: Yellow eyes are an ART severe sign.

questions.question: Akshay has been on ART for 3 months. He is well, developing well, weighs 12.5 kg and never misses a dose. His mother is pregnant again. What do you record and discuss?
points: No problems, no danger signs, no main symptoms
No malnutrition, developing well, takes all doses
Continue the same ART at the dose for his weight
Discuss the pregnancy and PMTCT, nutrition, family planning and adherence
Follow up in one month

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 8: Clinical staging
narrative: Use the WHO paediatric clinical staging. Which stage is each child?

questions.question: 4 years old with many lymph nodes over 0.5 cm in the axilla, groin and neck, without other cause.
6 months old with severe wasting that has not responded to treatment.
9 months old with PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA not responding to treatment, and herpes zoster.
questions.explain: Choose the highest stage that applies.

questions.question: 3 years old with persistent lymphadenopathy and recurrent SEVERE PNEUMONIA.
9 years old with Kaposi's sarcoma, otherwise well.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 8: Review questions
narrative: Answer the same questions as before the module, and see what you have learned.

questions.question: A child is under 16 months old. Which HIV test should be used, and why?
options: Serological, because it detects antibodies to the virus
Virological (PCR), because it detects the virus itself
Serological now, then confirm with PCR after 18 months

questions.question: Which follow-up treatment is critical for HIV-exposed and infected infants and children?
With no prevention, what is the overall risk that a mother passes HIV to her child in pregnancy, delivery and breastfeeding?
A 2-month-old breastfeeding baby has a positive virological (PCR) test. Is the child HIV-infected?
In the WHO 2014 module, when is a child with HIV eligible for ART?
options: Any child under five with confirmed HIV infection
Only children over 5 with a CD4 count below 350

questions.question: The mother is HIV-positive and the child is not confirmed infected. Where policy is breastfeeding with ARVs, what feeding is recommended?
options: Exclusive breastfeeding for as long as the child wants
Breastfeeding and formula together, for extra nutrition
Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, then complementary foods and breastfeeding to 12 months
questions.explain: Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, complementary foods from 6 months, and breastfeeding for the first 12 months. (The WHO answer, "exclusive breastfeeding until 12 months", was reworded: the module says exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months.)

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 8: Logbook test
narrative: You may use your chart booklet, but not the module. Circle the best answer.

questions.question: HIV:
What is an opportunistic infection?
options: An infection that takes advantage of a weak immune system to cause disease
An infection that takes advantage of an open wound
A disease for which home care is the only treatment

questions.question: Mother-to-child transmission of HIV can happen:
options: At delivery, and after birth when kissing the child
In pregnancy, at delivery, and after birth when hugging or holding the child
In pregnancy, at delivery, and after birth through breastfeeding

questions.question: With nothing done to prevent it, the chance of mother-to-child transmission is:
20 HIV-positive women with no interventions deliver 20 babies.
options: About 7 babies will be infected if the mothers breastfeed
About half will be infected if the mothers do not breastfeed at all
About two-thirds will be infected if the mothers stop breastfeeding at 6 months

questions.question: In advising about HIV care, you tell the caregiver and/or child:
options: ART can be taken at any time of day
ART must be taken every day for life, at the same times
Double the dose after a forgotten day

questions.question: In an infant of an HIV-infected mother, an antibody test can confirm infection when done at or after:
Sari, 2 months, breastfeeding, has a positive rapid antibody test. What do you do?
options: Start ART today and give feeding recommendations
Start cotrimoxazole, do a PCR test (and again at least 6 weeks after breastfeeding stops), and counsel on feeding
Do a PCR test today and plan a visit to give nevirapine

questions.question: Biki, 12 months, has a positive antibody test and is classified HIV EXPOSED. It is important that:
options: Cotrimoxazole is given until HIV is definitely ruled out
He is staged with the WHO paediatric staging
He gets nevirapine once a day

questions.question: Which of these is an ART severe sign?
Which of these medicines can cause a severe, possibly fatal skin reaction? Tick all that apply.
questions.explain: Cotrimoxazole (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), abacavir (hypersensitivity) and nevirapine. (The WHO key gives only ABC.)

questions.question: Maria, 4 weeks old, born at home to an HIV-positive woman with no interventions, is HIV EXPOSED and weighs 3.2 kg. Today you:
options: Give nevirapine 1.5 ml once daily only
Give nevirapine 1.5 ml once daily and cotrimoxazole 2.5 ml once daily
Give nevirapine 1.0 ml once daily and cotrimoxazole 2.5 ml once daily
questions.explain: An exposed infant starts cotrimoxazole from 4 to 6 weeks. (The WHO key gives nevirapine only.)

questions.question: Maria is later confirmed HIV-positive by PCR. You start:
options: First line: ABC or AZT + 3TC + LPV/r
Second line, because she is so young
Nothing: she is not yet eligible

questions.question: When Maria turns 3 years old, you:
options: Keep the same first-line medicines while she is stable

questions.question: What are the 5 As, in order?
points: Assess
Advise
Agree
Assist
Arrange

questions.question: Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis has reduced deaths of HIV-infected children.
All children under five with CONFIRMED HIV INFECTION should start ART, following the five steps.
questions.explain: (The logbook says "all children" and "6 steps"; the module has five steps, for children under 5.)

questions.question: At a follow-up visit on ART, you only re-assess the child if he looks unwell or the mother reports a problem.
Tina, 4 weeks old, born to an HIV-positive mother, not yet tested: you start cotrimoxazole today.
ART cures HIV after 2 years.
WHO recommends that HIV-positive mothers breastfeed exclusively for 6 months, then begin complementary feeding.
The CD4 count measures how much damage HIV has done to the immune system.
If an HIV-positive caregiver does not understand HIV and its treatment, adherence may be a problem.
Antiretroviral therapy is lifelong.
ART is given as a combination to fight HIV strongly and reduce the risk of resistance.

questions.question: Childhood injuries:

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 9: Exercise D (bonding and attachment)
narrative: Answer the questions about bonding and attachment.

questions.question: Bonding is:
options: The mother forming a relationship with her new baby, from the first hours after birth
The baby forming a relationship with the caregiver during the first two years

questions.question: Attachment happens especially at:

Sara notices that John is feeding less than usual. This is:
Name three consequences of poor attachment.
points: Difficulty trusting others
Depression or rage
Failure to thrive
Difficulty adapting to change
Behaviour problems and poor peer relations later
Poor problem solving and low self-esteem

narrative: Use the activity and milestone charts.

questions.question: Jyothi is 2 months old. Suggest play and communication.
points: Let her see, hear, feel, move freely and touch you
Move colourful things for her to see and reach; a shaker rattle
Smile, laugh and talk; copy her sounds

questions.question: Linus is 11 months old. Suggest play and communication.
points: Hide a toy and let him find it; peek-a-boo
Tell him the names of things and people
Teach gestures like waving bye-bye

questions.question: Which fine motor skills should a child of 2 years have?
options: Builds a tower of 6 cubes, undresses

questions.question: Which words should a child of 9 months say?
options: Mama, dada, and imitates one word

questions.question: Which social and adaptive skills should a child of 3 years have?
options: Dresses and undresses fully except buttons, counts to 10

questions.question: Ikupa, 36 months, walks only with support and says about 10 words. What do you do?
options: Refer for assessment of delayed development, within a few days

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 9: Exercise K (feeding recommendations)
narrative: Answer the questions about feeding.

questions.question: Which says "give foods that are high in energy and nutrient content in relation to volume" simply?
options: Give food that helps him grow without making him feel too full

questions.question: Which checking question follows "When will you begin giving these foods?" "When he is ready."
options: How will you know that he is ready?

questions.question: Why continue exclusive breastfeeding to 6 months?
options: Breast milk is the perfect food, well absorbed, and prevents infection

questions.question: A child of 6 up to 12 months who is breastfed needs:
options: 3 meals plus healthy snacks a day, breast milk first
5 meals a day and no breastfeeding

questions.question: A child of 2 years and older needs:
options: 3 family meals and 2 snacks a day

questions.question: An adequate serving means the child does not want any more after active feeding.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 9: Exercise L and M (immunization)
narrative: Use the national schedule.

questions.question: Why check the vaccination status of every child?
options: Every child should complete the schedule before the first birthday, and missed vaccines are given that day

questions.question: A 6-week-old did not get OPV at birth. Which OPV dose do you give?
questions.explain: OPV 0 is not given after 14 days.

questions.question: Salma is 4 months old. She had BCG and OPV 0 at birth, the 6-week vaccines (OPV 1, Penta 1, PCV 1, Rota 1, IPV 1) and the 10-week vaccines (OPV 2, Penta 2, PCV 2, Rota 2). Which vaccines does she need today, and when does she return?

Return at 9 months for MR, Men A and yellow fever
Bring the child health book every time; vaccinate the other children; explain the common reactions

questions.question: Khadija, 3 months, had BCG, OPV 0 and the 6-week vaccines 5 weeks ago. What does she need?
points: OPV 2, Pentavalent 2, PCV 2 and Rota 2 today
Return in 4 weeks for the 14-week vaccines

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 9: Exercise N (contraindications)
narrative: Decide whether to vaccinate today.

questions.question: A child who will be treated at home with antibiotics should be vaccinated today if due.
A child with very low weight should not be vaccinated.
questions.explain: Malnutrition is not a contraindication.

questions.question: A child who convulsed right after pentavalent 1 gets pentavalent 2 today.
questions.explain: Give the other vaccines, not pentavalent.

questions.question: A child with diarrhoea due for OPV gets it today, but the dose is not counted.
A child known to have AIDS with no vaccines gets all vaccines except BCG.
A child being referred urgently must be vaccinated before leaving.

questions.question: Jot, 26 months, had vitamin A 4 months ago. He needs vitamin A today.

No mebendazole today: the last dose was 3 months ago
Return in 3 months for mebendazole and in 6 months for vitamin A, up to 5 years
